modules.title: How computers, mobile devices and peripherals work
modules.summary: What computer components do and how to match a fault to its likely cause.

sections.heading: Follow information through the computer
paragraphs: Input devices capture information; processors execute instructions; memory holds the active working set; storage preserves files. RAM is volatile, so turning off power loses its contents. An SSD keeps data without power and normally improves file loading, but it cannot replace adequate RAM for many simultaneous applications. A CPU performs general processing, while a GPU handles highly parallel work such as graphics. The motherboard connects components through buses and expansion interfaces. A power supply converts incoming power into the voltages components require. Choose compatible sockets, memory generations and power requirements before upgrading.

sections.heading: Connections, mobile devices and printing
paragraphs: A connector’s shape does not guarantee its capabilities: a USB-C port may support different data speeds, charging levels or video features. Check specifications and test a known-good cable. Bluetooth handles nearby wireless peripherals; Wi-Fi connects devices to a local wireless network. Mobile systems balance performance against battery life and thermal limits. A swollen battery requires trained handling, not squeezing or puncturing. Printers can fail at the application, queue, driver, connection or mechanical stage. Laser printers use toner; inkjet printers spray liquid ink. A document appearing in a queue proves submission, not successful printing.

example.scenario: A laptop works normally but its external monitor shows no image through a new USB-C cable.
example.solution: Check whether the port and cable support video, select the correct monitor input, and test a known-good supported connection before replacing the display.

sections.heading: Diagnosing hardware faults
paragraphs: Start with safe, reversible checks: confirm power, inspect connections, read the exact error and reproduce the symptom. Shut down and follow manufacturer procedures before internal service; protect components from electrostatic discharge. Never open a power supply as a routine troubleshooting step. Distinguish capacity from speed: a nearly full disk and insufficient RAM can both slow a computer for different reasons. For printing, test another document and inspect the queue before reinstalling everything. A peripheral working on another computer narrows the cause toward the original device, driver or connection rather than proving every component healthy.

terms.definition: Volatile working memory used by active programs.
Software that lets an operating system communicate with hardware.
An attached input, output or storage device.

questions.prompt: Which component loses its working data when power is removed?
questions.explanation: RAM is volatile; persistent storage retains data without power.

questions.prompt: A matching USB-C connector guarantees which capability?
questions.explanation: Port and cable specifications determine features; shape alone does not.

questions.prompt: What is the safest first response to a visibly swollen laptop battery?
choices: Stop using it and seek approved service
questions.explanation: Damaged batteries require safe handling by qualified service personnel.

questions.prompt: What should you inspect before replacing a printer that prints nothing?
questions.explanation: Printing depends on the queue, connection, driver and printer state.

questions.prompt: A graphics-heavy task benefits particularly from which component?
questions.explanation: GPUs efficiently handle many graphics calculations in parallel.

modules.title: Operating systems, files and software
modules.summary: How operating systems manage files, permissions, software, and common faults.

sections.heading: What the operating system controls
paragraphs: An operating system allocates processor time, memory, storage and access to devices. Applications request those resources through system services rather than controlling every device directly. Processes are running programs; a service commonly works in the background. Virtual memory uses storage to extend the address space available to programs, but heavy paging can reduce performance. A file system organizes named files, folders and metadata. An extension suggests a file format; renaming an extension does not convert the underlying contents. Absolute paths identify a location from the root, while relative paths depend on the current location.

sections.heading: Installation, permissions and maintenance
paragraphs: Install software from trusted sources and verify operating-system, processor, memory and storage requirements. Standard user accounts reduce the damage an accidental or malicious action can cause. Administrative access should be used only when required. File permissions control who can read, change or execute information; permissions are separate from whether a file is hidden. Updates fix defects and vulnerabilities, while backups preserve recoverable copies. Cloud synchronization can spread deletion or corruption, so it is not automatically an independent backup. Before major changes, record the current configuration, protect important files and plan a rollback.

example.scenario: Only one user cannot save a document in a shared folder; other users can.
example.solution: Check that user’s effective permissions and available storage before reinstalling the application. The limited scope points toward account or folder access.

sections.heading: Diagnosing software and permission faults
paragraphs: Determine whether a problem affects one file, one application, one account or the whole machine. Observe resource usage and logs rather than guessing from a slow interface. Closing a hung process may recover responsiveness but can lose unsaved work. A safe restart is different from abruptly removing power. When an update causes a fault, check compatibility and use an approved recovery path. Avoid deleting unfamiliar system files to free space. Test the repaired workflow under the original user account and document the result; successful operation under an administrator account alone may hide the actual permission problem.

terms.definition: A running instance of a program.
The structure used to store and organize files.
Granting only the access needed for a task.

questions.prompt: Does renaming report.txt to report.pdf convert it into a PDF?
choices: No; the underlying format remains unchanged
Only if the file is small
questions.explanation: A format conversion must rewrite the file using the destination format.

questions.prompt: Which account is normally appropriate for routine daily work?
questions.explanation: A standard user account limits unnecessary privileges.

questions.prompt: What does high sustained paging often indicate?
questions.explanation: The system may be moving data between RAM and storage because active memory demand is high.

questions.prompt: Why is synchronization alone an incomplete backup strategy?
choices: It can replicate deletion or corruption
questions.explanation: Independent recoverable versions protect against mistakes that synchronization may propagate.

questions.prompt: One account cannot open a folder that others can use. What is a strong first hypothesis?
questions.explanation: A user-specific failure suggests permissions or account configuration.

modules.title: Troubleshooting and service-desk support
modules.summary: How to ask about a problem, test possible causes, and check the fix.

sections.heading: Ask questions and record the problem
paragraphs: An incident is an interruption or reduction in service. A service request asks for a standard item such as approved software or access. A problem investigation seeks the underlying cause of recurring incidents. Record the user, device, exact symptom, onset, impact and recent changes. Ask open questions first, then narrow them with specific tests. Prioritize using business impact and urgency: a shared checkout outage can outrank one employee’s cosmetic issue. Avoid asking users to expose passwords or unnecessary personal data. Explain what you are testing in language the user understands.

sections.heading: Test a hypothesis and restore service
paragraphs: Establish the scope, identify likely causes and choose the least disruptive test that distinguishes them. Change one variable at a time so the result is interpretable. Known-good components and accounts provide useful comparisons. Consult approved documentation and a knowledge base, but confirm that the article matches the environment. Workarounds can restore service while a root cause remains unresolved; record that distinction. Escalate when the issue exceeds your permissions, expertise, safety limits or agreed response commitments. Include evidence and steps already tried so the next technician does not restart blindly.

example.scenario: Everyone on one floor loses access to a server, while another floor still works.
example.solution: Investigate shared network equipment or the floor’s connection first. Reinstalling each user’s application would ignore the common failure boundary.

sections.heading: Confirm the fix and document it
paragraphs: After a fix, reproduce the original task with the user and check related functions that the change could affect. Record the cause when known, the action, validation and any follow-up. Useful metrics include first-response time, resolution time and repeat incidents; speed alone should not reward premature closure. Asset records track ownership, configurations and lifecycle status. Change management reviews risk and rollback before altering shared services. A service-level agreement defines service commitments rather than guaranteeing every incident vanishes instantly. Clear status updates and respectful listening remain part of the technical solution, especially during delays.

terms.definition: An unplanned service interruption or reduction in quality.
A temporary way to reduce impact without removing the underlying cause.
Transferring an issue to the appropriate authority or expertise.

questions.prompt: Which is the best first support note?
choices: Laptop A cannot reach shared drive since 9 a.m.; local files work
questions.explanation: Specific symptoms, timing and scope support diagnosis.

questions.prompt: Why change one troubleshooting variable at a time?
choices: To identify which change affected the result
questions.explanation: Controlled tests connect a change to its observed outcome.

questions.prompt: An alternate workflow restores service but leaves the root cause. This is a:
questions.explanation: A workaround reduces impact without necessarily eliminating the cause.

questions.prompt: When should an incident be closed?
choices: As soon as a command runs
After verifying the original task works and documenting the result
questions.explanation: Validation and documentation support reliable closure.

questions.prompt: Which incident usually deserves higher priority?
choices: A whole department unable to process orders
One typo in a help article
A request for a new wallpaper
questions.explanation: Broad business impact and urgency drive priority.

modules.title: Networks, addressing and physical connections
modules.summary: How devices connect, use addresses, and send data through network equipment.

sections.heading: From one device to a network
paragraphs: A local area network connects devices across a limited area; a wide area network connects networks over larger distances. A switch forwards Ethernet frames within a local network using MAC addresses. A router forwards packets between IP networks. A wireless access point connects wireless clients to the wired network; it is not automatically the internet connection itself. Client-server systems centralize services, while peer-to-peer arrangements let peers share directly. Star topologies connect endpoints to central equipment. A central switch failure can affect many clients, whereas one endpoint cable failure may affect only one.

sections.heading: Addresses, subnets and media
paragraphs: An IP address identifies an interface within an IP network. The subnet prefix describes which portion identifies the network, and the default gateway provides a path to destinations outside that subnet. IPv4 and IPv6 use different address structures; IPv6 is not simply an extra-fast form of Wi-Fi. Private IPv4 addresses are commonly translated at a network boundary using NAT. Copper Ethernet, fiber and wireless have different distance, interference, cost and installation tradeoffs. Fiber carries light and resists electromagnetic interference. Wireless uses shared radio spectrum, so walls, channel congestion and distance affect performance.

example.scenario: A computer can reach local shared files but cannot reach external websites by IP address.
example.solution: Check its default gateway and the upstream route. Local success shows that some LAN functions work; DNS alone cannot explain failure to reach a known external IP.

sections.heading: Checking network connections
paragraphs: Bandwidth is a link’s capacity, throughput is achieved data transfer, and latency is delay. A high-bandwidth link can still feel slow when latency or packet loss is high. Compare wired and wireless results to isolate radio issues. Verify physical link, address, subnet and gateway before blaming the application. Two devices using the same IP address can create intermittent connectivity. A connected Wi-Fi icon only confirms association, not successful internet access. Network diagrams should show devices, links and boundaries clearly enough that another person can trace the path from a client to a service.

terms.definition: A device that forwards frames within a local Ethernet network.
The router used to reach destinations outside the local subnet.
Delay experienced as data travels through a system.

questions.prompt: Which device primarily forwards packets between IP networks?
questions.explanation: Routing connects IP networks.

questions.prompt: What does a switch primarily use to forward Ethernet frames?
questions.explanation: Switches learn and use link-layer MAC addresses.

questions.prompt: Which medium is resistant to electromagnetic interference?
questions.explanation: Fiber transmits light instead of electrical signals.

questions.prompt: A Wi-Fi connection icon proves which statement?
choices: The client is associated with a wireless network
questions.explanation: Association does not establish that upstream services work.

questions.prompt: A link has high capacity but long delay. Which term describes the delay?
questions.explanation: Latency measures delay, separately from bandwidth.

modules.title: Network protocols and troubleshooting
modules.summary: The services and protocols involved in a network request, and how to troubleshoot them.

sections.heading: Why networks use layers
paragraphs: Layered models divide communication into responsibilities. Physical signaling carries bits; the data-link layer handles local frames; the network layer handles IP packets; transport provides communication between application endpoints. Application protocols define useful conversations such as requesting web content. The OSI model has seven layers, while TCP/IP groups responsibilities differently. Encapsulation adds control information as data moves down the stack; the receiver interprets and removes it. A layer model is a diagnostic aid, not a rule that every real fault belongs neatly to only one box.

sections.heading: Common services and their roles
paragraphs: DNS translates names into records such as IP addresses. DHCP can supply clients with addressing configuration automatically. HTTP defines web requests and responses; HTTPS protects HTTP in transit with TLS. TCP provides an ordered, reliable byte stream, while UDP sends datagrams without built-in delivery or ordering guarantees. Applications choose based on their needs and may add their own reliability. Ports distinguish services on an address: HTTPS commonly uses 443, HTTP 80 and DNS 53. Secure remote administration commonly uses SSH rather than unencrypted legacy alternatives. A reachable server can still reject an unauthorized application request.

example.scenario: A website loads when you enter its IP address but not when you use its name.
example.solution: Investigate DNS resolution and name-related configuration. The comparison suggests that at least one IP path works, though HTTPS certificates can complicate IP-only tests.

sections.heading: Testing each part of a network request
paragraphs: Ping tests one kind of reachability using ICMP; a blocked ping does not prove the host is down. A successful ping also does not prove that a web service is listening. Trace tools reveal responding hops, but some routers deliberately do not answer. Test progressively: physical connection, local address, gateway, remote destination, name resolution and application response. Distinguish a DNS error from a server’s HTTP error. Encryption protects data during transport, but it does not establish that a website’s claims are trustworthy. Never treat a familiar port number as proof that traffic is harmless.

terms.definition: A distributed naming service that resolves names to records.
A protocol that supplies network configuration to clients.
A transport protocol providing an ordered reliable byte stream.

questions.prompt: A hostname fails while its IP works. Which service is most directly implicated?
questions.explanation: DNS resolves names to address records.

questions.prompt: Which protocol supplies client IP configuration automatically?
questions.explanation: DHCP supplies addresses and related network settings.

questions.prompt: Which statement about UDP is accurate?
choices: It has no built-in delivery guarantee
It is a physical cable type
questions.explanation: UDP applications must handle reliability needs themselves.

questions.prompt: What does a successful ping prove?
questions.explanation: ICMP reachability does not prove application availability.

questions.prompt: Which default port is commonly associated with HTTPS?
questions.explanation: HTTPS conventionally uses port 443.

modules.title: Plan, segment and recover a business network
modules.summary: Planning a network around the business’s needs, limits, and recovery requirements.

sections.heading: Begin with business requirements
paragraphs: A good design begins with users, applications, locations, expected growth and availability needs. Record current devices and links, identify bottlenecks and distinguish measured demand from guesses. A network serving payment terminals and public guests needs different trust boundaries from a small isolated classroom lab. Draw both physical connections and logical networks. Estimate capacity for peak demand rather than only average activity. Compare purchase, licensing, maintenance, support and replacement costs. A design is defensible when each choice answers a requirement, including budget and support skills, rather than simply selecting the most expensive hardware.

sections.heading: Segmentation and resilience
paragraphs: A VLAN creates a logical broadcast domain on switching infrastructure. Routing connects VLANs, and access rules should permit only the necessary communication. Separating guest traffic from internal records reduces unnecessary exposure. Redundant power, links and equipment can reduce single points of failure, but redundancy adds cost and configuration complexity. A backup is a recoverable copy; failover keeps a service running on an alternate component. Recovery time objective describes acceptable restoration time, while recovery point objective describes acceptable data loss measured in time. Restore testing determines whether a recovery plan actually works.

example.scenario: A clinic allows visitors to use Wi-Fi and also transmits internal patient records.
example.solution: Separate guest and internal networks, restrict routes between them, secure administration and test permitted access. A second wireless name alone is insufficient without enforced isolation.

sections.heading: Operate and verify the design
paragraphs: Document address plans, device configurations, dependencies and responsible contacts. Use monitoring to track utilization, errors and availability against a baseline. Protect management interfaces and back up device configurations securely. Schedule changes, assess their impact and prepare a rollback. Acceptance tests should cover both ordinary work and chosen failure scenarios. Verify that users can reach required services and cannot reach prohibited ones. Common mistakes include assuming redundant links automatically provide independent paths, treating backups as tested when no restore has occurred, and omitting the ongoing labor needed to keep configurations and diagrams accurate.

terms.definition: A logical broadcast domain configured on switching infrastructure.
The target maximum time to restore a service after disruption.
The target maximum data-loss window expressed in time.

questions.prompt: What should drive the first network design decisions?
questions.explanation: Requirements connect technical choices to actual needs.

questions.prompt: Which goal is served by isolating guest traffic from internal systems?
questions.explanation: Segmentation limits access between trust zones.

questions.prompt: A restore can take four hours at most. Which target is described?
questions.explanation: RTO describes restoration time; RPO describes acceptable data loss.

questions.prompt: Which action best validates backups?
choices: Restoring representative data in a controlled test
questions.explanation: Recovery must be tested rather than inferred from file existence.

questions.prompt: Why document ongoing support cost?
choices: Maintenance and administration affect total cost
questions.explanation: Total cost includes the lifecycle effort required to operate the design.

modules.title: Recognize threats, vulnerabilities and risk
modules.summary: Common attacks, weaknesses they exploit, and ways to assess the risk.

sections.heading: Threats, vulnerabilities, and risk
paragraphs: An asset is something valuable, such as customer records or service availability. A threat is a possible cause of harm; a vulnerability is a weakness a threat could exploit. Risk combines the likelihood and impact of that harm. Confidentiality limits disclosure, integrity protects accuracy and authorized change, and availability keeps services usable. A stolen password can affect all three. Controls reduce risk but rarely remove it completely. A risk assessment considers the asset, plausible attacks, existing controls and consequences before choosing a response. Technical sophistication alone does not determine business impact.

sections.heading: Common attacks and warning signs
paragraphs: Phishing uses deceptive messages to prompt actions such as revealing credentials or opening malicious content. Social engineering exploits human trust, urgency or authority. Malware includes ransomware that denies access to data, spyware that collects information and other malicious programs. Unpatched software, weak access controls and unsafe defaults create opportunities. SQL injection occurs when untrusted input changes the meaning of a database query; parameterized queries separate data from executable instructions. Cross-site scripting can make untrusted content run as browser code. Defensive testing requires explicit authorization and a defined scope; curiosity is not permission to attack a real system.

example.scenario: An urgent email claims the principal needs gift cards and asks you to bypass normal approval.
example.solution: Verify through a known independent contact channel and follow purchasing procedures. The claimed authority and urgency are warning signs, not reasons to skip verification.

sections.heading: Assessing the risk
paragraphs: Distinguish an accidental disclosure from a deliberate intrusion, while recognizing that either can cause harm. Assess suspicious links without entering credentials or opening attachments. Report suspected incidents using the organization’s process. Security awareness is a control, but blaming users does not replace safer systems. Treating every risk as equally important wastes resources; prioritize severe plausible consequences. Risk can be reduced, avoided, transferred or accepted by an authorized decision maker. Insurance may transfer some financial consequences but does not prevent an attack or repair trust. Reassess as systems, threats and business needs change.

terms.definition: A weakness that can be exploited or triggered to cause harm.
Protection against unauthorized or accidental improper alteration.
Manipulation of people to obtain access or induce unsafe actions.

questions.prompt: An unpatched software flaw is best described as a:
questions.explanation: A flaw is a weakness; an attacker exploiting it is a threat.

questions.prompt: Which security objective concerns keeping records accurate?
questions.explanation: Integrity protects data from improper modification.

questions.prompt: What is the best response to an urgent unusual money request?
choices: Verify through an independent known channel
questions.explanation: Independent verification avoids trusting the suspicious channel.

questions.prompt: Which control directly helps prevent SQL injection?
questions.explanation: Parameterized queries keep input values separate from executable SQL.

questions.prompt: Buying cyber insurance primarily does what?
questions.explanation: Insurance addresses some consequences rather than preventing all incidents.

modules.title: Protect identities, systems and data
modules.summary: Access controls, encryption, backups, and other ways to protect data.

sections.heading: Control who can access systems and data
paragraphs: Authentication establishes an identity; authorization determines what that identity may do. Multifactor authentication combines different factor types, such as something known and something possessed. Two passwords are not two different factors. Least privilege gives a person or service only the rights its job requires. Role-based access assigns permissions through job functions. Review access when people join, change roles or leave. Shared accounts weaken accountability because actions are harder to attribute. A password manager supports unique credentials; a documented account recovery process reduces the temptation to bypass controls during an emergency.

sections.heading: Protect data across its lifecycle
paragraphs: Encryption transforms readable information into ciphertext using a key. Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret, while asymmetric systems use related public and private keys. Hashing creates a digest used for purposes such as integrity checks; it is not a reversible substitute for encryption. TLS protects communication in transit. Data at rest also needs appropriate protection and key management. Collect only necessary information, classify its sensitivity and limit retention. Firewalls filter traffic by policy; endpoint protection, patching, secure configuration and segmentation provide additional layers. A single product cannot supply every security function.

example.scenario: A club stores member contact information in a cloud spreadsheet shared with anyone who has the link.
example.solution: Limit sharing to authorized accounts, remove unnecessary fields, review editors and define retention. Encryption in transit would not correct overly broad sharing permissions.

sections.heading: Checking security controls
paragraphs: Choose controls for the risk and confirm they do not prevent legitimate work unnecessarily. A preventive control blocks an event, a detective control reveals it, and a corrective control helps restore a safer state. Logging detects activity only if records are collected, protected and reviewed. Physical access controls and secure disposal matter alongside software protections. Test authorization with both permitted and denied actions. Common errors include treating hashing as decryptable, assuming multifactor authentication makes phishing impossible, and believing a secure connection means the recipient should receive the data. Access policy and trustworthy handling remain necessary.

terms.definition: Establishing who or what is requesting access.
Deciding which actions an authenticated identity may perform.
A one-way digest used to represent data for comparison or integrity checks.

questions.prompt: Which question concerns authorization?
choices: May this user edit the payroll file?
questions.explanation: Authorization decides allowed actions after identity is established.

questions.prompt: Which pair uses distinct authentication factors?
questions.explanation: A memorized secret and a possessed device are different factor types.

questions.prompt: Which is ordinarily one-way rather than reversible?
questions.explanation: A cryptographic hash is not decrypted back into the original message.

questions.prompt: Why might HTTPS be insufficient to protect a shared document?
choices: Sharing permissions may still expose the document
questions.explanation: Transport encryption cannot correct excessive access rights.

questions.prompt: An alert that reports suspicious sign-ins is primarily a:
questions.explanation: An alert detects events rather than directly preventing them.

modules.title: Respond to incidents and maintain continuity
modules.summary: Preparing for incidents, containing damage, and restoring services.

sections.heading: Prepare before a disruption
paragraphs: Security operations turn policy into repeatable daily work. Maintain an inventory of assets, owners and critical services so alerts have context. Establish baselines for ordinary activity, collect useful logs and synchronize clocks. Vulnerability management identifies weaknesses, assesses priority, applies remediation and verifies the result. Patching should include testing and rollback appropriate to the system. Incident plans define decision makers, communications and escalation routes. Business continuity keeps essential operations functioning during disruption; disaster recovery focuses on restoring technology and data. Both require exercises, named responsibilities and accessible instructions.

sections.heading: Contain, investigate and recover
paragraphs: When an incident is suspected, follow the approved response plan rather than improvising a destructive cleanup. Confirm what is known and isolate affected resources when authorized to limit spread. Preserve logs and other evidence, record actions and maintain a chain of custody if formal investigation requires it. Eradication removes the cause; recovery restores trustworthy services and watches for recurrence. Notify the appropriate responsible people using established channels. Avoid promises about legal reporting deadlines without current jurisdiction-specific guidance. Evidence collection and service restoration can conflict, so the designated incident authority should direct priorities.

example.scenario: A workstation begins encrypting shared files.
example.solution: Escalate immediately and use the approved containment process to isolate the affected endpoint or access. Preserve relevant evidence and assess backups before restoring into an environment that may still be compromised.

sections.heading: Learn from the event
paragraphs: A post-incident review explains the timeline, impact, detection gaps and corrective actions without replacing evidence with blame. Assign owners and deadlines to improvements. Verify restored data, required permissions and application behavior before returning to normal work. Recovery point and recovery time targets help judge whether restoration met business needs. Common mistakes include restoring backups without removing the attack path, deleting logs before investigation, and confusing an absence of alerts with proof of safety. Test communication and manual workarounds too: a technically valid backup is less useful when staff cannot access the procedure or contact the recovery team.

terms.definition: Limiting the spread or impact of an incident.
A record of evidence handling, possession and transfers.
Maintaining essential operations through a disruption.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of incident containment?
questions.explanation: Containment reduces immediate harm while response continues.

questions.prompt: Which activity checks whether a patch solved the issue?
questions.explanation: Remediation should be followed by confirmation.

questions.prompt: What is the safest recovery approach after malware?
choices: Remove the cause, validate backups and restore through the response plan
questions.explanation: Recovery must avoid reintroducing the same compromise.

questions.prompt: Which record supports reliable evidence handling?
questions.explanation: Chain of custody records who handled evidence and when.

questions.prompt: Which task belongs in a post-incident review?
choices: Identifying improvements with owners and deadlines
questions.explanation: An actionable review improves future detection and response.

modules.title: Databases, information quality and business systems
modules.summary: Database relationships, data quality, access, and business information systems.

sections.heading: Organize data for a purpose
paragraphs: Data are recorded facts; information is data interpreted in context. A database organizes related data for retrieval and update. A relational table contains rows representing records and columns representing attributes. A primary key uniquely identifies a record. A foreign key links a record to a related table. Separating customers from orders avoids repeating the same customer details in every transaction. Normalization reduces avoidable duplication and update anomalies, though system designers may make documented performance tradeoffs. Choose data types and validation rules that reflect meaning, such as a date for an order date rather than arbitrary text.

sections.heading: Retrieve, protect and improve information
paragraphs: Queries select, filter, join, group and summarize records. A join connects related rows using a defined relationship; a careless many-to-many join can multiply results and distort totals. A transaction groups changes that should succeed or fail together, such as recording both sides of an inventory transfer. Backups, access permissions and audit trails support trustworthy operation. Data quality includes accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness and fitness for purpose. A required field can improve completeness without guaranteeing truth. Document a data dictionary so people interpret field definitions, codes and units consistently.

example.scenario: A customer’s address appears in 30 order records and changes next month.
example.solution: Store customer details once in a customer table and link orders using a customer ID. If historical shipping addresses must remain unchanged, preserve that transaction-specific information deliberately.

sections.heading: Connect systems to business decisions
paragraphs: Transaction processing systems record routine operations. Management reporting summarizes activity, while decision-support systems help analyze alternatives. Enterprise resource planning connects major functions through shared processes and data; customer relationship management organizes customer interactions. Integrations must reconcile identifiers, formats and ownership rather than merely moving files. Common mistakes include using names as guaranteed unique keys, calculating totals after an unintended duplicate join, and collecting fields no one needs. Ask who owns each dataset, how corrections occur and which decision the information supports. A technically successful import can still produce poor information if definitions disagree.

terms.definition: A field or field combination uniquely identifying a row.
A field linking a row to a related table.
Structuring relational data to reduce unnecessary duplication and anomalies.

questions.prompt: What uniquely identifies a row in a relational table?
questions.explanation: Primary keys uniquely identify records.

questions.prompt: Why separate customers and orders into related tables?
questions.explanation: Related tables reduce unnecessary duplication.

questions.prompt: A nonblank required field guarantees:
questions.explanation: Completeness and accuracy are different quality dimensions.

questions.prompt: What can an unintended many-to-many join do to totals?
questions.explanation: Repeated matches can duplicate values in an aggregate.

questions.prompt: A CRM system primarily supports:
questions.explanation: CRM organizes information about customers and interactions.

modules.title: Systems analysis, programming and testing
modules.summary: Turning a user’s requirements into software you can test and maintain.

sections.heading: Define the problem before the solution
paragraphs: Systems analysis investigates the current workflow, users, information and constraints. A functional requirement describes behavior, such as exporting a report. A nonfunctional requirement describes a quality or constraint, such as keyboard accessibility or response time. Interview users and observe the actual process; an assumed workflow can hide important exceptions. A feasibility study considers technical, financial, operational and schedule constraints. Model inputs, processing, outputs and error cases. A prototype explores a question cheaply, while an acceptance criterion states an observable condition for success. Neither a polished mockup nor working code automatically proves that the right problem was solved.

sections.heading: Build from clear programming concepts
paragraphs: Variables hold values, selection chooses a branch and iteration repeats work. Functions group behavior behind inputs and outputs. In object-oriented design, a class describes related data and behavior; an object is an instance. Encapsulation keeps implementation details behind an interface, inheritance derives a specialized form and polymorphism lets different implementations respond through a common interface. Prefer understandable models over elaborate hierarchies. Algorithms need correct boundary handling, suitable data structures and reasonable time and memory use. Version control records changes and supports collaboration; committing secrets makes them part of history even if a later change deletes them.

example.scenario: A ticket calculator charges a discounted price only when quantity is at least ten.
example.solution: Test quantities nine, ten and eleven. These boundary cases reveal whether the comparison correctly includes ten rather than checking only an ordinary large order.

sections.heading: Verify and maintain the system
paragraphs: Unit tests examine small pieces, integration tests check cooperation and acceptance tests validate user requirements. Test valid, invalid, empty and boundary inputs. Debugging traces why observed behavior differs from expected behavior; testing reveals a failure but does not always identify its cause. Maintenance includes fixes, security updates and adapting to changed needs. Document setup, dependencies and decisions someone else needs to operate the system. Common mistakes include implementing before clarifying requirements, treating compilation as proof of correctness, checking input only in the interface, and releasing an untested migration without a recovery plan.

terms.definition: An observable condition a solution must meet.
Keeping implementation details behind a defined interface.
A test at or near a limit where behavior changes.

questions.prompt: Which is a functional requirement?
choices: The system exports a CSV report
questions.explanation: Exporting a report describes required behavior.

questions.prompt: An object is:
questions.explanation: A class defines a type; objects are its instances.

questions.prompt: Which test best targets a discount beginning at quantity ten?
questions.explanation: Values around the threshold reveal boundary errors.

questions.prompt: What does successful compilation prove?
choices: The code passes the compiler’s checks
questions.explanation: Compilation is necessary in some languages but not a complete correctness test.

questions.prompt: Which testing level checks cooperation between components?
questions.explanation: Integration tests examine interacting parts.

modules.title: How web applications work
modules.summary: Browser requests, page structure, accessible forms, and data storage.

sections.heading: Follow a request from browser to server
paragraphs: A browser uses a URL to identify a resource and sends an HTTP request to a server. The server responds with a status, headers and usually content. HTML gives a page semantic structure, CSS controls presentation and JavaScript adds behavior. These roles cooperate rather than replacing one another. Client-side code runs in the user’s browser, while server-side code runs on infrastructure controlled by the application operator. Browser code is visible to the user, so private API keys and access decisions cannot safely depend on keeping it secret. An API defines an interface through which software exchanges data or requests operations.

sections.heading: Build a usable, resilient interface
paragraphs: Semantic headings, real buttons, labels and meaningful link text help people and assistive technology understand a page. Keyboard users need a visible focus indicator and a sensible interaction order. Responsive layouts adapt to available space without hiding required content. Forms should explain constraints and show specific errors beside the relevant fields. Validate on the server as well as in the browser, because browser checks can be bypassed. Handle loading, empty and failure states explicitly. A useful interface remains understandable when a request fails; it does not silently discard a student’s work.

example.scenario: A registration form marks errors only by turning field borders red.
example.solution: Add a written error message associated with each field and preserve entered values. Color alone does not explain the correction and may be inaccessible.

sections.heading: Storage, security and common mistakes
paragraphs: Cookies, local storage and server databases serve different purposes. Local storage persists in one browser but can be unavailable or cleared; it is unsuitable as the sole home of important shared records. Treat user input as untrusted, encode output for its context and use parameterized database queries. Authentication and authorization must protect sensitive server operations. Cache static resources thoughtfully and measure performance on constrained devices. Common mistakes include using clickable generic elements instead of buttons, trusting hidden form fields, assuming a successful network response means valid business data, and promising cross-device synchronization when information exists only in one browser.

terms.definition: Markup describing the semantic structure of a web document.
A defined interface for software interactions.
Layout behavior that adapts to different available screen sizes.

questions.prompt: Which technology provides semantic page structure?
questions.explanation: HTML communicates document structure and meaning.

questions.prompt: Where must a private server API key be protected?
choices: On the server, outside public client code
questions.explanation: Anything delivered to a browser can be inspected by its user.

questions.prompt: Why validate form data on the server?
questions.explanation: The server must enforce rules independently of client behavior.

questions.prompt: What is a limitation of local storage?
choices: It can be cleared or unavailable in that browser
questions.explanation: Local browser storage is not guaranteed durable or cross-device.

questions.prompt: Which error treatment is most accessible?
choices: Specific text linked to the affected field
questions.explanation: Text explains the issue and can be associated with assistive technology.

modules.title: Probability, distributions and uncertainty
modules.summary: Distributions, probability, sampling, and what you can conclude from data.

sections.heading: Describe a distribution before drawing conclusions
paragraphs: A population is the full group of interest; a sample is the subset observed. The mean adds values and divides by their count. The median is the middle of sorted values and is less affected by extreme observations. The mode is the most frequent value. Range describes the difference between maximum and minimum, while standard deviation summarizes typical spread around the mean. Histograms show distributions of numerical data; bar charts compare categories. Examine shape, unusual values and units before choosing a summary. A high average does not imply that every observation is high.

sections.heading: Reason about probability
paragraphs: Probability ranges from zero to one. For equally likely outcomes, an event’s probability is favorable outcomes divided by all possible outcomes. Independent events do not change one another’s probabilities; mutually exclusive events cannot occur together. These are different ideas. Conditional probability asks about an event given additional information. A test can be highly accurate yet produce many false alarms when the condition is rare. Expected value multiplies each outcome by its probability and adds the results; it is a long-run average, not a guaranteed result for one attempt. Use counts or a two-way table to make probability relationships concrete.

example.scenario: Three delivery times are 2, 3 and 16 days.
example.solution: The mean is 7 days, while the median is 3 days. Report the unusually long delivery as well as the summary; the mean alone hides the typical experience.

sections.heading: Sampling and inference pitfalls
paragraphs: Random sampling helps reduce selection bias, but a large sample can still be biased if it systematically excludes important groups. Correlation describes association, not proof that one variable causes another. A confounder can influence both. Statistical significance does not establish practical importance, and failing to find significance does not prove no effect exists. Confidence intervals express uncertainty in estimates under stated methods; do not read them as a guarantee about each individual observation. Common mistakes include averaging percentages with different denominators, treating missing values as zero, and comparing groups collected through incompatible methods.

terms.definition: The middle value after observations are ordered.
Probability of an event given specified information.
A variable that influences both an apparent cause and an outcome.

questions.prompt: Which summary resists a single extreme outlier better?
questions.explanation: The median depends on ordering rather than the magnitude of an extreme value.

questions.prompt: What is the mean of 2, 3 and 16?
questions.explanation: Their sum is 21; dividing by three gives 7.

questions.prompt: Independent events are events that:
choices: Do not change one another’s probabilities
questions.explanation: Independence differs from mutual exclusivity.

questions.prompt: What does correlation alone establish?
questions.explanation: Other explanations can produce an association.

questions.prompt: A huge sample drawn only from volunteers may still suffer from:
questions.explanation: Sample size does not fix systematic selection problems.

modules.title: Collect, clean, analyze and communicate data
modules.summary: How to collect and clean data, check calculations, and present the results.

sections.heading: Start with a question and a data plan
paragraphs: Define the decision, target population, unit of observation and measurement before collecting data. Distinguish numerical measurements from categories, and discrete counts from continuous quantities. Record provenance: who collected the data, when, how and under which definitions. A CSV is a plain-text table exchange format; a workbook can contain formulas, formatting and multiple sheets. SQL retrieves structured records; Python, R and spreadsheets can transform and analyze them. Select tools based on dataset size, reproducibility and the task. Keep an untouched raw copy so corrections and transformations can be audited.

sections.heading: Clean the data and check calculations
paragraphs: Check missing values, duplicate records, impossible ranges, inconsistent categories and mismatched units. Decide and document how each issue will be handled. A missing sale is not automatically a zero sale. Standardize dates and identifiers before merging datasets. Sorting changes order; filtering changes the visible subset. A pivot table summarizes data by categories, but its result depends on the aggregation selected. Relative spreadsheet references move when copied, while absolute references lock a row or column. Calculate percentage change as new minus old, divided by old; a zero baseline requires a different description.

example.scenario: A club’s attendance rises from 40 to 50 members.
example.solution: The increase is 10 members, or 10 ÷ 40 = 25%. Dividing by the new value would answer a different question and understate this growth rate.

sections.heading: Present results accurately
paragraphs: Choose a chart that fits the question: lines for ordered time trends, bars for category comparisons and scatterplots for relationships between numerical variables. Label units, period, source and relevant uncertainty. Truncated bar axes can exaggerate differences; a line chart may use a narrower scale if it is clearly labeled and justified. Separate results from interpretation and limitations. Provide a recommendation that the evidence supports rather than inventing certainty. Common mistakes include claiming causation from a trend, reporting many decimal places unsupported by measurement quality, and making a chart attractive while leaving the denominator or comparison group undefined.

terms.definition: A record of where data came from and how it was produced.
A tool for grouping and aggregating tabular data.
The change divided by the original value, expressed as a percentage.

questions.prompt: Why preserve a raw data copy?
questions.explanation: An unchanged original allows transformations to be checked.

questions.prompt: Attendance rises from 40 to 50. What is the percentage increase?
questions.explanation: The increase is 10 divided by the original 40.

questions.prompt: Which chart usually fits a monthly sales trend?
questions.explanation: Ordered time trends are commonly shown with a line chart.

questions.prompt: What should a missing measurement automatically become?
choices: No value until a justified handling rule is chosen
questions.explanation: Missingness has meaning and should not be silently recoded.

questions.prompt: What does an absolute spreadsheet reference preserve when copied?
questions.explanation: Dollar signs can lock reference coordinates.

modules.title: Machine learning, evaluation and AI reasoning
modules.summary: Learning methods, model evaluation, and the limits of AI predictions.

sections.heading: Match the learning method to the task
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence is a broad field concerned with tasks such as perception, reasoning and decision-making. Machine learning builds patterns from data instead of hand-writing every rule. Supervised learning uses labeled examples: classification predicts categories, while regression predicts numerical values. Unsupervised learning explores structure such as clusters without supplied target labels. Reinforcement learning uses feedback from actions toward a reward. A feature is an input representation and a label is the target in supervised learning. Training data quality and relevance constrain what a model can learn; more data is not automatically better data.

sections.heading: Evaluate on information the model has not seen
paragraphs: Separate training, validation and test data so model selection does not contaminate the final evaluation. Overfitting learns details that fail to generalize; underfitting misses useful structure. Leakage occurs when information unavailable at prediction time enters training or evaluation. Accuracy is correct predictions divided by all predictions. Precision measures how often positive predictions are correct; recall measures how many actual positives are found. Choose metrics based on the cost of mistakes. A model that always predicts the majority class can appear accurate while failing the very cases that matter.

example.scenario: Only 2% of transactions are fraudulent. A model labels every transaction legitimate.
example.solution: It achieves 98% accuracy but zero recall for fraud. Evaluate the confusion matrix, precision, recall and the costs of missed fraud before calling it useful.

sections.heading: Representation, reasoning and limitations
paragraphs: Models represent information through features, rules, graphs, vectors or learned parameters. Computer vision interprets images; natural language processing works with language. Search explores candidate states or solutions, while rule systems apply explicit conditions. Generative models produce plausible content from learned patterns but can produce false statements. Monitor deployment for drift when data or behavior changes. Human review, suitable uncertainty and limits on automated action matter in consequential settings. Common mistakes include calling every automated rule machine learning, testing on training examples, optimizing one metric without business context and presenting a confident generated explanation as verified evidence.

terms.definition: Learning patterns too specific to training data to generalize well.
The share of actual positive cases identified as positive.
Use of information that should be unavailable to a prediction or evaluation.

questions.prompt: Predicting a house price is ordinarily:
questions.explanation: Regression predicts a numerical value.

questions.prompt: Grouping customers without target labels is commonly:
questions.explanation: Clustering explores structure without supplied outcome labels.

questions.prompt: Why keep final test data separate?
choices: To estimate performance on unseen examples
To remove the need for validation
questions.explanation: A held-out test supports a less contaminated performance estimate.

questions.prompt: A fraud model predicts no fraud in a dataset with rare fraud. What can be misleading?
choices: The number of actual fraud cases
questions.explanation: Majority-class predictions can yield high accuracy while missing all positives.

questions.prompt: Information from after an outcome is used to predict that outcome. This is:
questions.explanation: Future information would not be available at the intended prediction time.

modules.title: Privacy, AI fairness and responsible information use
modules.summary: Privacy, consent, bias, and who is responsible for decisions made with data.

sections.heading: Privacy is a design decision
paragraphs: Personal information can identify a person directly or become identifying when combined with other records. Data minimization means collecting only what a defined purpose requires. Explain collection and use clearly, control access and retain information only as long as justified. Removing names does not necessarily anonymize a dataset if dates, locations or other details allow reidentification. Consent should be meaningful rather than buried in confusing language, and some uses may require additional legal authority. Privacy and security overlap but differ: securely storing unnecessary sensitive information can still be an inappropriate privacy practice.

sections.heading: Check fairness and accountability
paragraphs: Bias can enter through historical data, sampling, labels, selected objectives and deployment conditions. A dataset that underrepresents a group can make performance estimates unreliable for that group. Compare relevant error rates and consequences, not only one overall score. Fairness measures can conflict, so document the chosen goal and its tradeoffs. Explain who owns a system, who can challenge an outcome and how corrections occur. Intellectual property and licensing constrain reuse even when content is publicly visible. Generative AI assistance still requires checking facts, source permissions and the specific competition’s rules on outside help.

example.scenario: A club trains a participation predictor using only students who already attend meetings.
example.solution: The sample excludes nonparticipants, so it cannot fairly describe all students. Reconsider the data plan and purpose before using the model to decide whom to invite.

sections.heading: Consent, privacy, and AI claims
paragraphs: Use a practical review: identify the purpose, necessary fields, affected groups, likely harms, protective controls and an accountable decision maker. Provide human review when errors could materially affect people. Distinguish explaining a model from proving that it is correct or fair. A statistically useful proxy can still reproduce sensitive distinctions. Avoid uploading private member records into unapproved tools. Common mistakes include assuming public access grants unrestricted reuse, treating name removal as complete anonymization, and describing an algorithm as neutral merely because it uses mathematics. Review real outcomes after deployment as well as before launch.

terms.definition: Collecting and retaining only information necessary for a defined purpose.
Connecting supposedly anonymous data back to an individual.
Systematic differences in model behavior that can create unfair outcomes.

questions.prompt: What is data minimization?
choices: Collecting only data needed for a defined purpose
questions.explanation: Purpose and necessity guide collection and retention.

questions.prompt: Removing names from records guarantees anonymity:
choices: No; combinations of other fields may identify people
Whenever the file is a spreadsheet
questions.explanation: Indirect identifiers can enable reidentification.

questions.prompt: Which is a strong fairness evaluation practice?
choices: Compare meaningful outcomes and errors across affected groups
questions.explanation: Group-specific performance and harms can be hidden in averages.

questions.prompt: A publicly visible article may be copied freely because it is visible:
choices: No; reuse rights still need checking
questions.explanation: Access and copyright permission are different.

questions.prompt: Who remains responsible for checking generated claims used in a project?
choices: The person or team using them
questions.explanation: Using an AI tool does not remove responsibility for accuracy and rules.

modules.title: Initiate and plan a project
modules.summary: Setting a project’s scope, assigning responsibilities, and planning the work.

sections.heading: A project has an outcome and an ending
paragraphs: A project is a temporary effort that creates a unique result. Operations are ongoing activities that sustain the organization. A project charter authorizes the effort and summarizes purpose, objectives, major constraints and responsibility. Identify stakeholders early: they can influence the work or be affected by it. The sponsor supplies support and authority, while the project manager coordinates delivery. Define measurable success criteria and distinguish outputs from outcomes. Printing 200 brochures is an output; increasing attendance may be an outcome. Clear scope states what work is included so enthusiasm does not silently expand the commitment.

sections.heading: Break work into manageable pieces
paragraphs: A work breakdown structure divides deliverables into smaller components. Estimate tasks, resources, dependencies and duration with the people who understand the work. A milestone marks an important point rather than a duration of effort. The critical path is the longest dependent path through the schedule; delay on it can delay the project unless the plan changes. Budget for realistic costs and contingency. Identify risks before they become issues, assign owners and plan responses. Predictive planning defines substantial work in advance; adaptive approaches use feedback and shorter cycles when requirements or solutions are uncertain.

example.scenario: A fundraiser needs two days of design, then three days of printing, then one day of distribution.
example.solution: Those dependent tasks require at least six days in sequence. Assigning more people to distribution does not shorten the earlier design and printing dependencies automatically.

sections.heading: Scope, estimates, and project risks
paragraphs: Write acceptance criteria that someone can verify: 'report contains a reconciled budget and three sourced recommendations' is stronger than 'report is great.' Build a communication plan around who needs which information and when. A responsibility matrix clarifies who performs, approves or advises on work, preventing duplicate effort and missing decisions. Do not confuse effort with elapsed duration or assume every task can run simultaneously. A risk is uncertain; an issue is already occurring. Planning should be sufficient for the project’s size and uncertainty, then updated as evidence changes rather than treated as an unchangeable prediction.

terms.definition: The boundaries of the work and deliverables included in a project.
The longest dependent sequence determining the minimum schedule duration.
A person or group affecting or affected by a project.

questions.prompt: Which activity is a project?
choices: Creating a new chapter website by a defined date
questions.explanation: A unique temporary effort differs from ongoing operations.

questions.prompt: Who typically provides high-level authority and support?
questions.explanation: The sponsor authorizes and supports the effort.

questions.prompt: Dependent tasks take two, three and one days. Minimum sequence duration is:
questions.explanation: Sequential dependencies add to six days.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes a risk rather than an issue?
choices: The venue might cancel next month
questions.explanation: A risk is an uncertain future event.

questions.prompt: Which acceptance criterion is most verifiable?
choices: The report includes a reconciled budget and three sourced recommendations
questions.explanation: Observable evidence supports acceptance.

modules.title: Execute, monitor and close a project
modules.summary: Tracking progress, handling changes, and handing over a finished project.

sections.heading: Coordinate work and monitor evidence
paragraphs: Execution produces the planned deliverables and coordinates people, resources and suppliers. Monitoring compares actual progress, cost, quality and risk against the agreed plan. A status report should identify what is complete, what is next, which decisions are needed and which issues threaten the outcome. A task being 90% complete for several weeks is weaker evidence than a finished, accepted deliverable. Quality assurance improves the process used to produce work; quality control inspects the results. Team leadership includes resolving disagreements, clarifying responsibilities and removing obstacles rather than merely collecting updates.

sections.heading: Handle change and uncertainty
paragraphs: A change request should describe the proposed adjustment and its effects on scope, time, cost, quality and risk. Obtain approval through the project’s agreed authority before treating the change as a commitment. Scope creep is uncontrolled expansion. Adaptive teams can reprioritize a backlog within a defined process, but flexibility does not mean unlimited resources. Track issues, owners and actions separately from potential risks. Escalate decisions the team cannot make. If a supplier delay affects the critical path, evaluate alternatives such as resequencing, reducing scope or adding appropriate resources; each has costs and limits.

example.scenario: Two days before a report is due, a stakeholder requests an additional survey of 300 students.
example.solution: Estimate effort and impact, explain the tradeoff and seek an authorized scope or deadline decision. Silently accepting the request hides a predictable delivery risk.

sections.heading: Hand over and close the project
paragraphs: Closure verifies deliverables against acceptance criteria, obtains approval, transfers ownership and records unresolved items. Reconcile spending, archive useful records and release resources. Capture lessons about both successful practices and failures so future projects can act on them. Benefits may appear after closure, so name the person responsible for measuring them. A deployment is not finished if no one can maintain or use it. Common mistakes include declaring completion when work is merely submitted, hiding overruns, confusing extra features with required quality and leaving handover instructions or account ownership with someone who is leaving the organization.

terms.definition: Uncontrolled expansion of a project’s work or requirements.
A proposal evaluated for its impact before authorized change.
Transfer of the result and its operating responsibility to an owner.

questions.prompt: A project’s deliverables expand without review. This is:
questions.explanation: Uncontrolled expansion is scope creep.

questions.prompt: What should a change decision consider?
choices: Scope, time, cost, quality and risk
questions.explanation: Changes have interacting consequences.

questions.prompt: Which is stronger evidence of progress?
choices: An accepted deliverable meeting defined criteria
questions.explanation: Accepted outputs are observable rather than merely estimated.

questions.prompt: What is required at project closure?
choices: Acceptance, handover and useful archived records
questions.explanation: Closure ensures the result can be operated and the effort accounted for.

questions.prompt: Quality control primarily concerns:
questions.explanation: Quality control inspects deliverables.

modules.title: Public institutions, policy and ethical service
modules.summary: How public organizations make policy, provide services, and answer to the community.

sections.heading: Public purposes and levels of government
paragraphs: Public organizations provide services and carry out policies under authority granted through public institutions. Federal, state and local governments have different responsibilities, and some services involve multiple levels working together. Legislative bodies make laws and authorize spending, executive organizations administer programs, and courts interpret law and resolve disputes. The exact allocation depends on the jurisdiction. Public managers balance effectiveness, efficiency, equity, legality and accountability. Unlike a business, an agency cannot define success only as profit. A service can be essential even when the people most in need cannot pay its full cost.

sections.heading: Follow a policy from problem to evaluation
paragraphs: Public policy begins with identifying a problem, understanding affected groups and comparing possible responses. Options may include direct service, regulation, incentives or partnerships. Analyze evidence, costs, expected benefits and unintended effects before recommending a choice. Implementation translates a decision into staffing, procedures, communication and delivery. Evaluation examines whether outcomes improved and for whom. Stakeholder engagement should reach more than the most vocal participants. Public communication uses clear language, accessible formats and accurate explanations of eligibility, process and appeal options. Informing people is different from collecting meaningful feedback that can influence a decision.

example.scenario: A town proposes moving a bus stop to save travel time.
example.solution: Compare travel benefits with accessibility and safety effects for riders, especially people who cannot easily walk farther. Ask affected users and evaluate outcomes after implementation.

sections.heading: Ethics, accountability and management
paragraphs: A conflict of interest occurs when a personal interest could improperly influence an official responsibility. Disclose potential conflicts and use the organization’s recusal process rather than assuming good intentions solve the problem. Stewardship means using entrusted resources responsibly. Transparency supports scrutiny, while legitimate privacy and security needs still require protection. Keep accurate records and apply procedures consistently. Common mistakes include treating equal treatment as always equivalent to equitable access, promising a policy without authority or funding, and using service volume as the only measure of success. Measure service quality, public outcomes and access alongside cost and speed.

terms.definition: A course of action adopted to address a public issue.
The obligation to explain and take responsibility for decisions and results.
A personal interest that could improperly influence official duties.

questions.prompt: Why is profit alone inadequate for evaluating an agency?
choices: Public goals include access, legality and community outcomes
questions.explanation: Public organizations serve goals beyond financial return.

questions.prompt: Which step checks whether a policy achieved its intended results?
questions.explanation: Evaluation examines outcomes after implementation.

questions.prompt: A purchasing official’s relative owns a bidder. What is appropriate?
choices: Disclose the conflict and follow recusal rules
questions.explanation: Disclosure and appropriate separation protect impartiality.

questions.prompt: Which public communication practice is strongest?
choices: Use clear, accessible explanations and feedback channels
questions.explanation: Accessible communication helps people understand and use services.

questions.prompt: What should a service evaluation consider besides cost?
questions.explanation: Public performance includes the effects on the community.

modules.title: Public budgets, revenue and performance
modules.summary: How governments raise money, set budgets, and report results.

sections.heading: How public budgets differ from personal budgets
paragraphs: A public budget authorizes and plans the use of resources for community purposes. Revenues can include taxes, fees, grants and other receipts; their availability and legal restrictions vary. Expenditures fund services, staff, supplies and capital assets. An operating budget supports recurring activities, while a capital budget plans long-lived investments. Budget authority is not identical to cash in the bank. A restricted grant cannot automatically be moved to an unrelated program. Public finance requires understanding who can authorize commitments and which rules govern procurement, spending and reporting.

sections.heading: Compare costs, results and funding choices
paragraphs: Distinguish fixed costs from costs that change with service volume. Cost per service unit divides relevant spending by the number of units, but it does not measure quality by itself. A program can lower unit cost by serving easier cases while neglecting people with complex needs. Cost-benefit analysis compares costs and valued benefits; cost-effectiveness compares ways to achieve an outcome when benefits are difficult to price. Debt can finance long-lived assets but creates future repayment obligations. A one-time grant should not be treated as permanent recurring funding without a plan for continuing expenses.

example.scenario: A tutoring program spends $12,000 and delivers 600 sessions.
example.solution: Average cost is $20 per session. To evaluate value, also examine learning outcomes, session quality and whether students with the greatest need can access the service.

sections.heading: Controls and honest reporting
paragraphs: Internal controls such as authorization, separation of duties and reconciliations reduce errors and misuse. Procurement specifications should define needs clearly so offers can be evaluated fairly. Competitive selection processes protect accountability, but exact requirements must be checked for the jurisdiction. Monitor budget-to-actual results and explain material variances. An output counts activity, such as permits processed; an outcome measures the effect, such as reduced unsafe construction. Common mistakes include equating spending the entire budget with success, ignoring lifecycle maintenance costs of a new asset and reporting a favorable average while hiding unequal access or declining service quality.

terms.definition: A plan for recurring service and administrative activities.
A plan for long-lived investments and assets.
The difference between planned and actual results.

questions.prompt: A recurring staff salary belongs primarily in which budget?
questions.explanation: Operating budgets support recurring activities.

questions.prompt: A $12,000 program provides 600 sessions. Average cost per session is:
questions.explanation: Divide $12,000 by 600 sessions.

questions.prompt: Why is a one-time grant risky as the sole funding for permanent staff?
choices: The grant may end while recurring costs continue
questions.explanation: Recurring commitments need sustainable funding.

questions.prompt: Which measure is an outcome rather than an output?
questions.explanation: An outcome describes an effect, not just activity.

questions.prompt: Why separate payment approval from reconciliation when practical?
choices: To reduce errors and misuse through independent checks
questions.explanation: Separation of duties reduces unchecked control over transactions.

modules.title: Healthcare organizations, people and quality
modules.summary: Care settings, staffing, communication, and quality improvement.

sections.heading: Organizations and the continuum of care
paragraphs: Healthcare organizations include hospitals, outpatient clinics, long-term care facilities, public health agencies and other services. Primary care addresses common needs and ongoing coordination; specialty care focuses on a particular condition or field. Preventive care aims to reduce disease or detect problems earlier. Care transitions move a person between settings and can create information gaps. Administrators coordinate staffing, facilities, scheduling and resources so clinical professionals can deliver care. Administrative decisions affect patient experience and safety, but an administrator should not substitute unqualified judgment for licensed clinical decisions. Different ownership structures can influence governance and funding without eliminating responsibility for quality.

sections.heading: People, strategy and communication
paragraphs: Workforce planning matches skills, credentials and staffing to service demand. Orientation, continuing training, supervision and clear roles support safe practice. Recruitment alone cannot solve retention problems caused by poor scheduling or an unsafe workplace. Strategic planning links community needs and organizational capacity to measurable priorities. Communicate changes with patients and staff using accessible language; confirm understanding rather than assuming a message was received. Standardized handoffs can reduce missing information at transitions. Effective leadership encourages staff to report near misses so the organization can learn before a preventable harm occurs.

example.scenario: A clinic has long waits even though daily visit totals are stable.
example.solution: Map arrivals, check-in, rooming and clinician availability by time of day. The bottleneck may reflect scheduling and uneven capacity rather than too few total staff hours.

sections.heading: Structures, strategy and technology
paragraphs: Functional structures group people by specialty; matrix structures combine reporting relationships; multidivisional structures separate major services or locations. A chief medical officer leads medical matters, a chief nursing officer nursing practice and a chief financial officer financial stewardship. SWOT compares internal strengths and weaknesses with external opportunities and threats; PEST examines political, economic, social and technological conditions. Telehealth enables remote services but still needs suitable access, privacy and clinical judgment. Clinical information systems support care, while PACS stores and retrieves medical images. Fee-for-service pays for individual services; value-based models connect payment to defined quality and cost goals. HMOs generally emphasize network-based coordinated care, PPOs usually offer more out-of-network flexibility and POS plans combine features; actual terms vary.

sections.heading: Quality and process improvement
paragraphs: Quality includes safety, effectiveness, timeliness, patient-centeredness, efficiency and equity. Measure the process before changing it, choose an intervention and check the result. A root-cause analysis examines system contributors rather than stopping at 'someone made a mistake.' Track both intended outcomes and balancing measures, such as whether shorter visits increase callbacks. Patient satisfaction is useful but cannot alone establish clinical quality. Common mistakes include treating every delay as a staffing shortage, using averages that hide underserved groups and discouraging reporting to make incident counts appear low. Support a culture that distinguishes learning from concealment.

terms.definition: Connected services across a person’s different health needs and settings.
An event that could have caused harm but did not.
The step whose limited capacity constrains a process.

questions.prompt: Which activity is primarily an administrator’s responsibility?
questions.explanation: Administrators organize resources and operations within their role.

questions.prompt: A near miss should be:
choices: Treated as proof of no risk
questions.explanation: Near misses reveal risks before harm occurs.

questions.prompt: What should happen before changing a slow clinic workflow?
choices: Map the process and measure the bottleneck
Assume every role needs more staff
questions.explanation: Measurement helps locate the actual constraint.

questions.prompt: Patient satisfaction alone establishes clinical quality:
questions.explanation: Satisfaction is one measure among safety, effectiveness and other dimensions.

questions.prompt: Why use standardized handoffs?
choices: To reduce missing information during transitions
questions.explanation: Handoffs support continuity and reliable communication.

questions.prompt: Which system primarily stores and retrieves medical images?
questions.explanation: PACS is a picture archiving and communication system.

modules.title: Healthcare finance, insurance and information
modules.summary: Healthcare billing, insurance, budgets, and patient records.

sections.heading: Follow the revenue cycle
paragraphs: The revenue cycle spans scheduling and registration through billing, payment and reconciliation. Accurate patient and coverage information helps prevent avoidable delays. Coding represents documented services in standardized forms; billing uses that information to submit a claim. A claim is a request for payment, not proof that payment is guaranteed.
