Payers review coverage, documentation and other requirements. Denials need analysis and an appropriate correction or appeal rather than repeated submission of unchanged errors. Distinguish the amount charged, the amount allowed by an agreement and the amount ultimately collected. These figures are not interchangeable.

sections.heading: Insurance and budget basics
paragraphs: A premium maintains insurance coverage. A deductible is an amount a covered person may need to pay before specified benefits apply; a copayment is a stated charge and coinsurance is a percentage share. Actual obligations depend on the plan and service, so avoid universal promises. Administrators budget labor, supplies, facilities, technology and other costs. Fixed costs can remain over a relevant range of volume, while variable costs change with activity. Compare actual revenue and spending with the budget and investigate significant variances. Cash flow matters because a service may incur costs well before a claim is paid.

example.scenario: A simplified plan applies 20% coinsurance after the deductible is met to an allowed $500 service.
example.solution: The patient share under those assumptions is $100, and the payer share is $400. Do not apply the percentage to an unrelated list price or ignore remaining plan conditions.

sections.heading: Policy, safeguards and public programs
paragraphs: HIPAA’s Privacy Rule governs protected health information use and disclosure; its Security Rule addresses electronic protected information through administrative, physical and technical safeguards. The Breach Notification Rule covers required notices after qualifying breaches. These rules apply to covered entities and business associates, not automatically to every person who knows a health fact. The Anti-Kickback Statute targets knowing, willful remuneration for federally reimbursed referrals or business; Stark addresses specified physician self-referrals involving financial relationships unless an exception applies. Medicare is federal insurance mainly for older adults and some eligible younger people. Medicaid is jointly funded federally and by states and administered by states under federal requirements. CMS administers major coverage programs within HHS; CDC focuses on public health. OSHA addresses worker safety, including bloodborne-pathogen exposure controls, training and safer work practices. Compliance translates these duties into policies, audits, reporting and corrective action.

sections.heading: Technology, policy and trustworthy records
paragraphs: Electronic health records organize clinical information, while practice-management systems support scheduling and administrative workflows. Interoperability means systems can exchange and meaningfully use information, not merely send a file. Role-based access, audit logs, secure communication and appropriate retention protect sensitive records. Privacy laws and payer requirements must be checked through current authoritative guidance; a study summary cannot replace compliance advice. Common mistakes include assuming all staff need access to every record, treating software as a cure for poor documentation and using billing codes to imply services that records do not support. Accuracy and ethical stewardship connect finance, care and trust.

terms.definition: A request to a payer for payment of a covered service.
A percentage share of an eligible cost paid by the insured person.
The ability of systems to exchange and meaningfully use information.

questions.explanation: Usable meaning matters as well as transport.

questions.explanation: The HIPAA Security Rule addresses administrative, physical and technical safeguards for ePHI.

questions.explanation: The Anti-Kickback Statute targets prohibited remuneration for covered referrals and business.

modules.title: Agribusiness economics, finance and marketing
modules.summary: Farm markets, seasonal budgets, contracts, and business risks.

sections.heading: How agribusinesses work together
paragraphs: Agribusiness includes input suppliers, producers, processors, distributors, retailers and service organizations. A farm is one part of this larger chain. Inputs such as seed, feed, labor and equipment become outputs sold into markets. Demand reflects consumers’ willingness and ability to buy; supply reflects producers’ willingness and ability to sell. Weather, disease, energy prices and trade conditions can shift supply or demand. Many biological production processes take time, so producers cannot instantly adjust output when prices change. Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative use of a scarce resource such as land or labor.

sections.heading: Use budgets and market information
paragraphs: An enterprise budget estimates revenue and costs for a particular activity. Revenue equals quantity sold multiplied by price, but profit requires subtracting all relevant costs. Distinguish cash costs from noncash costs such as depreciation. Break-even price equals total relevant cost divided by units sold. Working capital supports seasonal expenses before harvest receipts arrive. Market research examines buyers, quality requirements, channels and competition. Commodity marketing often emphasizes standardized grades and volume; differentiated products may compete on origin, attributes or service. A contract can allocate delivery and price risk, but its obligations must be understood before agreement.

example.scenario: A school greenhouse expects to sell 800 plants and has $2,400 in relevant costs.
example.solution: Break-even average price is $2,400 ÷ 800 = $3 per plant. If only 600 plants sell, that same cost requires $4 per plant, illustrating volume risk.

sections.heading: Ownership, contracts and environmental obligations
paragraphs: Sole proprietorships center ownership in one person; partnerships share ownership; corporations are separate legal entities; cooperative members organize for mutual benefit. Liability and tax treatment depend on the form and jurisdiction. Contracts define quantity, quality, price, delivery and remedies for nonperformance. Agribusiness legal issues also include employment, product responsibility, land use and environmental duties. Environmental law addresses effects on air, water, soil, habitats and people. EPA rules vary by farm activity: pesticide use, waste handling and discharges can involve different requirements. FIFRA regulates pesticides, and label directions are part of lawful use; registration does not authorize every imaginable application. Trade opens markets and access to inputs but adds currency, shipping and policy exposure. Precision sensors and other technology can improve decisions only when data and maintenance are dependable.

sections.heading: Ethics and management decisions
paragraphs: Accurate weights, truthful claims, fair dealing and responsible labor practices build trust. Business arrangements involve contracts, ownership and liability, but exact legal duties depend on current jurisdiction and the activity. Use qualified guidance for real decisions. Manage risk through suitable diversification, insurance, safety, reserves and sound operations rather than assuming one tool removes all uncertainty. Common mistakes include treating sales as profit, ignoring family labor or equipment wear in economic analysis and planning from an unusually favorable season alone. Evaluate a range of yield and price outcomes and explain the assumptions behind a recommendation.

terms.definition: An estimate of revenue and costs for a particular production activity.
The value of the best alternative forgone.
Relevant total cost divided by the units expected to be sold.

questions.prompt: Agribusiness includes:
choices: Input suppliers, producers, processors and distribution businesses
questions.explanation: Agribusiness spans the agricultural value chain.

questions.prompt: Costs of $2,400 spread over 800 plants imply which break-even price?
questions.explanation: $2,400 divided by 800 equals $3.

questions.prompt: What is the opportunity cost of using land for one crop?
choices: The value of its best alternative use
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost represents the forgone alternative.

questions.prompt: Why use several yield and price scenarios?
choices: To assess exposure to uncertain outcomes
questions.explanation: Scenarios show how results depend on uncertain inputs.

questions.prompt: Revenue is $10,000 and relevant costs are $8,000. Profit is:
questions.explanation: Profit equals revenue minus costs.

questions.prompt: Why must an agricultural operator check rules for its specific activities?
choices: Requirements vary with activities such as pesticide use, discharge and waste handling
questions.explanation: Environmental duties depend on the actual activity and applicable authority.

modules.title: Agricultural operations, safety and natural resources
modules.summary: Production schedules, equipment, safety, and natural resource management.

sections.heading: Plan biological and physical operations
paragraphs: Agricultural operations combine production schedules, labor, equipment, storage and biological processes. Capacity is not unlimited: planting windows, animal needs and weather can constrain when work happens. Standard operating procedures describe repeatable safe steps, while records make results traceable. Inventory includes inputs and harvested products; perishable goods need suitable temperature, handling and rotation. Quality control checks whether products meet specifications. Traceability connects a product to its source, handling and destination so an issue can be investigated and affected lots identified. Efficient operations reduce avoidable loss without hiding defects or bypassing safety.

sections.heading: Stewardship and workplace safety
paragraphs: Soil, water, energy and biodiversity are productive resources as well as environmental concerns. Erosion removes soil; conservation practices can reduce losses and preserve long-term productivity. Nutrient management matches inputs to need rather than assuming more fertilizer always improves yield. Water planning considers availability, timing, quality and efficient application. Integrated pest management combines monitoring, prevention and appropriate control decisions. Follow product labels and applicable safety rules, use appropriate protective equipment and keep untrained people away from hazardous equipment. Never infer that a 'natural' substance is automatically safe or that protective equipment replaces hazard reduction.

example.scenario: A harvest lot has a suspected storage-temperature problem.
example.solution: Identify and hold the affected lot, review temperature and handling records and follow the approved safety process. Mixing it with other lots destroys traceability and can spread the problem.

sections.heading: Natural cycles and emergency readiness
paragraphs: Plants and animals depend on interacting water, nutrient and energy cycles. Decomposition returns nutrients to soil; runoff can carry nutrients away and damage water systems. Production decisions should account for these feedbacks, seasonal growth and resource limits. Safety planning identifies hazards, trains workers and provides a way to report noncompliance without hiding it. During an emergency, protect people, alert the designated responders and follow the trained procedure rather than improvising a hazardous rescue. Agricultural insurance can cover specified financial losses subject to policy terms; prevention and contingency planning remain necessary.

sections.heading: Manage for long-term performance
paragraphs: Compare output, input use, waste, product quality and safety incidents rather than chasing yield alone. Preventive equipment maintenance can reduce breakdowns during a narrow production window. Train workers, communicate hazards and assign responsibility for inspections and records. Sustainability involves economic viability, environmental stewardship and social responsibility; one favorable metric does not establish all three. Common mistakes include using averages that hide spoiled lots, treating environmental impacts as unrelated to business costs and solving a recurring problem only after each failure. Use records to identify patterns, then test improvements and verify that product quality and safety remain protected.

terms.definition: The ability to follow a product’s source, handling and movement.
A monitoring-based combination of prevention and appropriate pest controls.
Responsible management of resources entrusted to someone.

choices: To trace affected products if a problem arises
questions.explanation: Lot records connect products to their production and handling history.

questions.prompt: Which approach supports long-term soil productivity?
choices: Matching conservation and nutrient practices to conditions
questions.explanation: Stewardship protects resources while supporting production.

questions.prompt: What should happen to a suspected unsafe lot?
choices: Hold and identify it through the approved process
questions.explanation: Isolation and records support safe investigation.

questions.prompt: Personal protective equipment:
choices: Is one control within a broader safety system
questions.explanation: Safety also depends on hazard reduction, procedures and training.

questions.prompt: Why schedule preventive maintenance before a critical production period?
choices: To reduce breakdown risk during limited operating windows
questions.explanation: Maintenance helps preserve capacity when timing is constrained.

modules.title: Property, ownership and real-estate markets
modules.summary: Property rights, ownership, valuation, and real estate careers.

sections.heading: Property includes rights as well as land
paragraphs: Real estate includes land and improvements attached to it. Real property refers to associated ownership interests and rights, while personal property generally describes movable items. A fixture began as personal property but became attached in a way that may make it part of the real estate; facts, agreements and applicable law matter. Ownership rights are often described as a bundle that can include possession, use, exclusion and transfer, subject to lawful restrictions and others’ rights. An easement grants a particular use of another person’s land. A lien is a claim securing an obligation, not necessarily a right to occupy the property.

sections.heading: Property descriptions and market value
paragraphs: A deed transfers an ownership interest; title describes ownership rights and claims rather than simply naming one piece of paper. Legal descriptions identify a parcel more precisely than a casual street address. Land-use controls, private restrictions and physical conditions can affect permitted use. Supply, demand, location, condition and available financing influence markets. An appraisal is an informed opinion of value for a stated purpose and date, not a guarantee of a selling price. The sales-comparison approach uses comparable properties and justified adjustments; the cost and income approaches answer different valuation questions.

example.scenario: Two similar homes sold for different prices; one sale occurred after a major renovation.
example.solution: Investigate condition, date, terms and location before treating the prices as interchangeable comparables. A valuation needs relevant evidence and reasoned adjustments.

sections.heading: Careers and professional roles
paragraphs: Sales agents help clients market, find and negotiate property within their authorized role. Brokers meet additional licensing requirements and may supervise agents; exact requirements vary by state. REALTOR is a membership designation associated with the National Association of REALTORS, rather than a synonym for every licensee. Professional associations can provide education, standards and networking. Property managers oversee ongoing operation and leasing, appraisers develop value opinions and mortgage professionals arrange financing. Residential property serves housing needs, while commercial niches include offices, retail and industrial uses. Appurtenances are rights or features belonging with property; hereditaments are property interests capable of inheritance.

sections.heading: Ownership and valuation mistakes
paragraphs: Distinguish a leasehold right to occupy from ownership of the property. An encumbrance affects rights or interests but does not always prevent transfer. Zoning permission does not automatically satisfy every permit, covenant or safety requirement. Review source documents and use qualified professionals for actual transactions; definitions here are educational and exact state rules can differ. Common mistakes include confusing a deed with a mortgage, assuming attached equipment always transfers regardless of an agreement, and equating asking price with market value. Read the question’s stated property rights and facts before selecting an answer based on ordinary everyday language.

terms.definition: A defined right to use another person’s property for a particular purpose.
A claim against property securing an obligation.
An informed opinion of value for a specified purpose and date.

questions.explanation: Real estate includes land and attached improvements.

questions.explanation: An easement grants a particular use of another property.

choices: An opinion of value for a stated purpose and date
The same as an asking price

choices: Condition differences can require justified adjustments

modules.title: Transactions, mortgages and property calculations
modules.summary: The steps in a property sale, mortgage costs, and common calculations.

sections.heading: A transaction has stages and conditions
paragraphs: A real-estate transaction commonly moves from negotiation to agreement, due diligence, financing and closing. A contract states the parties’ obligations, property, terms and conditions. A contingency makes performance depend on a specified event such as financing or inspection; exact rights depend on the agreement and governing law. Earnest money demonstrates commitment under agreed handling terms, while escrow involves a neutral arrangement for holding money or documents until conditions are met. Inspections evaluate condition; title work examines ownership-related claims. Closing reconciles documents and funds and completes the transfer according to applicable procedures.

sections.heading: Understand mortgage and investment arithmetic
paragraphs: A mortgage loan creates a repayment obligation secured by property. Principal is the amount borrowed or remaining; interest is the borrowing charge. An amortizing payment gradually reduces principal, though the interest and principal shares change over time. Loan-to-value ratio divides loan amount by the property value used by the lender. Equity is property value minus outstanding secured debt, before selling costs and other adjustments. A down payment is not the same as total closing cash because fees and other items can also apply. For income property, net operating income subtracts operating expenses from operating revenue before financing and income taxes.

The secondary mortgage market involves trading existing mortgage loans or related securities, which can provide lenders with funds for further lending. It is distinct from the primary market where a borrower obtains a new loan.

example.scenario: A buyer finances $240,000 of a property valued at $300,000.
example.solution: Loan-to-value is $240,000 ÷ $300,000 = 80%. The $60,000 difference is a 20% down payment in this simplified example, before closing costs.

sections.heading: Checking property calculations
paragraphs: Read the basis of every percentage: a commission calculated on sale price differs from an interest charge calculated on outstanding principal. Simple annual interest is principal multiplied by annual rate and time in years, but actual loan disclosures may use more complex payment conventions. Compare financing using total relevant costs and terms rather than a payment alone. Lower payments can result from a longer repayment period that increases total interest. Common mistakes include treating gross rent as profit, assuming approval removes every contingency and presenting an illustrative calculation as a current loan offer or individualized financial recommendation.

terms.definition: The amount borrowed or remaining unpaid on a loan.
Loan amount divided by the property value used for lending.
A contract condition tied to a specified event.

questions.prompt: A $240,000 loan on $300,000 value has what LTV?
questions.explanation: Divide the loan by the value: 240,000 ÷ 300,000.

questions.prompt: Which amount is the principal?
questions.explanation: Principal is the debt amount rather than the borrowing charge.

questions.prompt: Why can a lower monthly payment still cost more overall?
choices: A longer term may create more total interest
questions.explanation: Time and total cost matter alongside payment size.

questions.prompt: Gross rent is the same as net operating income:
choices: No; operating expenses must be considered
questions.explanation: NOI subtracts operating expenses from operating revenue.

questions.prompt: A financing contingency concerns:
choices: A contract condition related to obtaining financing
questions.explanation: Contingencies establish conditions under the contract.

modules.title: Agency, disclosure and ethical transactions
modules.summary: Who an agent represents, what they must disclose, and how local rules apply.

sections.heading: Know whom the professional represents
paragraphs: Agency is a relationship in which an agent acts for a principal within authorized duties. A client is represented; a customer may participate without that same representation. The distinction affects what duties and services are owed. Fiduciary responsibilities commonly involve loyalty, care, accounting, disclosure, confidentiality and obedience to lawful instructions, but exact requirements vary. Authority can be limited, so an agent cannot promise actions outside the agreement. Clarify representation and obtain required disclosures before assumptions create a conflict. A commission arrangement by itself does not explain every duty or prove that every participant is represented.

sections.heading: Disclosure, conflicts and fair dealing
paragraphs: Material information can influence a reasonable transaction decision. Know which facts require disclosure and which information must remain confidential under applicable rules. Do not invent an answer when uncertain; consult the responsible professional or current authoritative requirements. Representing parties with competing interests can create conflicts requiring special treatment or may be restricted. Fair housing principles prohibit unlawful discrimination in housing-related activity. Ethical communication focuses on the property and objective needs rather than steering people through stereotypes. Advertising should be truthful, authorized and sufficiently clear that a reasonable reader is not misled. Funds held for others require proper handling and records.

example.scenario: A buyer asks a seller’s representative to reveal the seller’s lowest acceptable price.
example.solution: The representative should explain the representation relationship and protect confidential negotiating information unless disclosure is authorized or required. Helpfulness does not override duties to the principal.

sections.heading: Fair housing and layered regulation
paragraphs: The federal Fair Housing Act identifies race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status and disability as protected bases. Discriminatory refusal, different terms and steering can affect access; state or local protections can add requirements. Federal lead-disclosure rules generally require known lead-paint and hazard information before sale or lease of most pre-1978 housing. Other disclosures depend on law and facts, so do not assume every hazard follows the same rule. Licensing, zoning, leases, tenant protections and local permits involve different regulatory authorities. Buyers’ agents represent buyers, sellers’ agents represent sellers, and dual or subagency arrangements require careful treatment under applicable rules.

sections.heading: Checking duties and local requirements
paragraphs: Separate ethical principles from a claim about a specific state deadline, form or license rule. Use the current official event guide for the test’s expected scope and current regulators for real activity. When a question presents a conflict, identify the principal, duty, known fact and proper authorization before choosing a response. Common mistakes include assuming a friendly agent represents everyone, confusing confidentiality with permission to conceal a required material disclosure and following a client’s unlawful instruction. Accurate records and candid explanations protect all parties more effectively than vague assurances that everything will work out.

terms.definition: The person or organization represented in an agency relationship.
A duty to act with the required loyalty and care for another’s interests.
Information important enough to affect a reasonable decision.

questions.prompt: In agency, the represented party is the:
questions.explanation: An agent acts for a principal.

questions.prompt: A client instructs an agent to discriminate unlawfully. The agent should:
choices: Obey because every instruction is binding
Refuse unlawful conduct and follow proper professional procedures
questions.explanation: Duties do not require obedience to unlawful instructions.

questions.prompt: Why clarify representation early?
choices: To avoid mistaken assumptions about whom the agent serves
questions.explanation: Representation defines duties and potential conflicts.

questions.prompt: Confidentiality means an agent may always conceal required material disclosures:
choices: No; confidentiality and disclosure obligations must both be respected
questions.explanation: The applicable duties must be reconciled rather than reduced to absolute secrecy.

questions.prompt: What should an agent do when uncertain about a required disclosure?
choices: Consult current requirements and responsible professional guidance
questions.explanation: Current authoritative guidance is needed for jurisdiction-specific obligations.

questions.prompt: Which is a federally protected Fair Housing Act basis?
questions.explanation: Disability is one of the statutory protected bases.

modules.title: Supply chains, operations and inventory
modules.summary: How goods, information, and money move from suppliers to customers.

sections.heading: See the whole supply chain
paragraphs: A supply chain connects suppliers, producers, distributors, retailers and customers. Goods often move toward customers, while information and money move in several directions. Operations transform inputs into useful outputs. Supply-chain management coordinates these activities so local improvements do not damage the overall result. A factory can appear efficient by making enormous batches while creating excess inventory elsewhere. Forecasts estimate future demand; actual orders provide different evidence. The bullwhip effect describes amplified demand variation upstream when organizations react to distorted or delayed information. Shared timely information and sensible ordering policies can reduce avoidable swings.

sections.heading: Inventory benefits and costs
paragraphs: Inventory can include raw materials, work in process, finished goods and supplies needed to operate. Cycle stock supports normal replenishment, while safety stock buffers uncertainty. Carrying inventory ties up money and creates storage, damage and obsolescence costs. Too little inventory can cause stockouts and lost service. A reorder point combines expected demand during replenishment lead time with any chosen safety stock. Inventory turnover compares cost of goods sold with average inventory value, using compatible accounting units. Physical counts and cycle counts check records against reality; accurate records are essential for dependable planning.

example.scenario: A shop uses 12 units daily, receives replenishment after five days and keeps 15 units of safety stock.
example.solution: A simple reorder point is 12 × 5 + 15 = 75 units. This assumes the stated demand and lead time model; different uncertainty requires a more careful policy.

sections.heading: Check the effect on the whole supply chain
paragraphs: Capacity is the output a process can sustain under stated conditions. A bottleneck constrains the flow, so improving a nonconstraint may not increase overall output. Lean approaches reduce waste and improve flow; just-in-time arrangements need reliable processes and suppliers rather than magical zero-risk inventory. Quality should be built into work, with checks that detect defects before they travel downstream. Common mistakes include treating all inventory as waste, comparing turnover using sales revenue against cost-valued inventory and maximizing machine utilization when customer demand does not need the extra output. Evaluate service, quality, cost and resilience together.

terms.definition: Inventory held as a buffer against uncertainty.
The inventory level that triggers a replenishment order.
Amplification of demand variation as information and orders move upstream.

questions.prompt: Which inventory buffers uncertainty?
questions.explanation: Safety stock cushions variation in demand or lead time.

questions.prompt: Daily demand is 12, lead time five days and safety stock 15. Reorder point is:
questions.explanation: Expected lead-time demand is 60; add 15.

questions.prompt: What is a bottleneck?
choices: The capacity constraint limiting process flow
questions.explanation: A bottleneck constrains throughput.

questions.prompt: Which behavior can create waste despite high machine utilization?
choices: Producing excess goods customers do not need
questions.explanation: Local utilization can worsen excess inventory and total performance.

questions.prompt: Inventory turnover calculations should compare:
choices: Revenue with any arbitrary stock number
questions.explanation: Cost of goods sold and average inventory should use compatible valuation.

modules.title: Purchasing, supplier selection and responsible sourcing
modules.summary: Writing purchasing requirements, comparing suppliers, and checking performance.

sections.heading: Turn a need into a purchasing specification
paragraphs: Purchasing obtains goods and services needed by the organization. A useful specification states function, quantity, quality, delivery needs and relevant acceptance requirements without unnecessary restrictions. Clarify the requirement before seeking offers. A requisition asks internally for a purchase; a purchase order communicates an authorized order to a supplier. Receiving checks what arrived against the order and agreed standards. Invoice matching compares billing with the order and receipt to reduce errors and unsupported payment. Separate requesting, approving and reconciling duties where practical so no one person controls an entire transaction unchecked.

sections.heading: Evaluate more than the sticker price
paragraphs: Total cost of ownership includes purchase price plus relevant transport, installation, operation, support, quality and disposal costs. Supplier evaluation can consider capacity, delivery reliability, quality, financial stability, ethical practices and support. Use criteria and evidence consistently. A low price can be expensive if defects shut down operations. Single sourcing can simplify coordination but creates dependency; multiple sources can improve resilience while adding coordination cost. Negotiate clear terms and responsibilities. Contracts allocate obligations and risk but do not eliminate the need to monitor actual performance or resolve ambiguity before a problem becomes urgent.

example.scenario: Supplier A charges $900 but needs $250 freight. Supplier B charges $1,050 with freight included; quality and delivery are otherwise equal.
example.solution: Comparable delivered costs are $1,150 and $1,050, making B $100 lower. Confirm other relevant costs before calling the quoted price the full cost.

sections.heading: Manage ethics and relationships
paragraphs: Maintain appropriate confidentiality and avoid gifts or personal interests that could distort selection. Disclose conflicts through the organization’s process. Responsible sourcing considers labor conditions, environmental effects and lawful practices alongside operational needs. Scorecards can track on-time delivery, defect rates and responsiveness, using definitions both parties understand. Collaborate on root causes rather than accepting repeated emergency expediting as normal. Common mistakes include choosing the cheapest unit price without lifecycle costs, changing specifications after offers without a fair process and treating a long relationship as a reason to stop checking supplier performance. Evidence and clear expectations support trust.

terms.definition: An authorized order stating goods or services and agreed terms.
All relevant costs of acquiring, using and disposing of an item.
A structured record of supplier performance against defined measures.

questions.prompt: What should happen before requesting supplier offers?
choices: Define the purchasing need and specification
questions.explanation: Clear specifications make offers relevant and comparable.

questions.prompt: A $900 item plus $250 freight costs:
questions.explanation: Add the relevant delivered costs.

questions.prompt: Which is part of total cost of ownership?
choices: Purchase, use, maintenance and disposal costs
questions.explanation: Total cost considers the relevant lifecycle.

questions.prompt: Why match an invoice with the order and receipt?
choices: To check that billing matches authorized goods actually received
questions.explanation: Matching helps detect errors and unsupported payment.

questions.prompt: What should a buyer do about a personal relationship with a bidder?
choices: Disclose it and follow conflict procedures
questions.explanation: Disclosure protects impartial selection.

modules.title: Distribution, transportation and returns
modules.summary: Transport, storage, order fulfillment, and returns.

sections.heading: Distribution connects the network
paragraphs: Distribution places products where and when customers need them. Warehouses store, handle and prepare goods; distribution centers often emphasize flow and order fulfillment. Receiving, put-away, picking, packing and shipping each create opportunities for error or delay. Layout and identification should support safe movement and accurate selection. Cross-docking transfers suitable goods from inbound to outbound movement with little storage, but it requires coordination. Packaging protects the product and communicates handling information, while its weight and volume affect cost. Distribution planning should consider customer location, order size, delivery frequency and product characteristics rather than simply minimizing the number of buildings.

sections.heading: Compare transport options
paragraphs: Road, rail, water, air and pipeline offer different combinations of speed, flexibility, capacity and cost. Air is often fast but expensive; water can move large international volumes economically but slowly. Rail is useful for suitable high-volume routes, while road transport offers flexible local access. Intermodal transportation combines modes. Lead time includes more than travel: order processing, waiting, handling and customs can matter. Track reliability as well as average speed. A cheaper slow mode can require more inventory, so compare total logistics cost and service risk rather than freight price in isolation.

example.scenario: A slower transport option saves $400 in freight but requires $550 more inventory and spoilage cost.
example.solution: Under those estimates, total relevant cost rises by $150. Choose using the full service and cost picture, not the freight saving alone.

sections.heading: Track deliveries and returns
paragraphs: Useful measures include order accuracy, on-time delivery, damage, fulfillment time and total cost per order. Define 'on time' against an agreed promise rather than moving the deadline after delivery. Reverse logistics handles returns, repairs, reuse, recycling and disposal. Returned items require identification and condition checks before being put back into saleable stock. Plan for disruption through alternative routes, suitable buffers and clear communication. Common mistakes include speeding shipping to compensate for avoidable warehouse delays, ignoring last-mile constraints and assuming every return has no value. Trace the full order cycle to find the actual cause of missed service.

terms.definition: Moving goods from inbound to outbound flow with little or no storage.
Movement using more than one transport mode.
Managing returns, repairs, reuse, recycling and disposal flows.

questions.prompt: Which activity is reverse logistics?
choices: Receiving a customer return for inspection
questions.explanation: Returns and recovery flows are part of reverse logistics.

questions.prompt: What does intermodal transport involve?
questions.explanation: Intermodal movement combines modes.

questions.prompt: Freight saves $400 but other relevant costs rise $550. Total cost:
questions.explanation: The $550 increase exceeds the $400 saving by $150.

questions.prompt: Why measure reliability as well as average transport speed?
choices: Variable delivery can disrupt planning even when the average is acceptable
questions.explanation: Uncertainty can require buffers or cause missed promises.

questions.prompt: What should happen before a returned item reenters saleable stock?
questions.explanation: Returned products need appropriate quality and safety checks.

modules.title: Programming foundations in Python
modules.summary: A runnable beginner sequence: variables and types, input and output, conditions, loops, functions, lists and dictionaries, scope, and splitting a program into modules.

sections.heading: Why one language, and how to run it
paragraphs: The concepts in this lesson exist in every language, but learning them in one language first makes practice concrete. This lesson uses Python 3 because its syntax is short and readable and it is free. Install Python from python.org, then save code in a file such as grades.py and run it from a terminal with python grades.py (or python3 on macOS and Linux). A free editor such as Visual Studio Code or IDLE, which comes with Python, works well.
Competitive events usually allow any language that meets the requirements. Check the current guide for platform, packaging, and judging requirements before choosing.

sections.heading: Variables, types, input, and output
paragraphs: A variable is a name for a value. Python's basic types are int (whole numbers), float (decimals), str (text), and bool (True or False). input() always returns text, so convert it before doing math. f-strings insert values into text and can format them, such as two decimal places with :.2f.

code.content:
name = input("Your name: ")
bill = float(input("Bill total: "))
people = int(input("Number of people: "))
tip_rate = 0.18

share = bill * (1 + tip_rate) / people
print(f"{name}, each person pays ${share:.2f}")

bullets: Entering 60 for the bill and 4 people prints "each person pays $17.70" because 60 x 1.18 / 4 = 17.70.
Entering "four" for people raises a ValueError. The next lesson shows how to handle bad input.

sections.heading: Conditions, loops, and functions
paragraphs: if, elif, and else choose between paths. A for loop repeats once for each item in a sequence; a while loop repeats as long as a condition is true. A function packages steps under a name, takes parameters, and returns a result, which makes code reusable and testable. Name functions with verbs that say what they do.

Lists hold ordered items: scores = [92, 88, 95]. Dictionaries map keys to values: {"Ana": [92, 88, 95]}. Variables created inside a function are local, meaning they exist only inside it; this scope rule prevents functions from accidentally changing each other's data.

example.scenario: Trace the program above. What does it print?
steps: Ben: (78 + 85 + 80) / 3 = 243 / 3 = 81.0, which is at least 80 but below 90, so "B".
example.solution: It prints "Ana: 91.7 (A)" and "Ben: 81.0 (B)". Tracing by hand like this is the most useful debugging habit for beginners.

sections.heading: Organize code into modules and debug
paragraphs: As a program grows, split it into modules (separate .py files) by responsibility: one for data, one for calculations, one for the user interface. Import functions where they are needed: from grading import average. Keep the main program short and readable. A common pattern ends the main file with if __name__ == "__main__": main(), so the file can be imported for testing without running.

Debugging is systematic. Read the error message's last line and the line number. Reproduce the problem with the smallest input. Print or inspect variable values before the failing line. Change one thing at a time and retest. Common beginner bugs include off-by-one loop ranges, forgetting to convert input() text to numbers, using = instead of ==, and indentation that puts a line inside or outside a loop by mistake.

practice.task: Write a function count_passing(scores, cutoff=70) that returns how many scores are at or above the cutoff. Then call it on [65, 70, 88, 59, 91] and print the result.

A named, reusable block of code that can take inputs and return a result.
A collection that maps keys to values.

questions.explanation: Local scope keeps function data separate.

modules.title: Saving data, validating input, handling errors, and testing
modules.summary: Store data in files or a database, check input for format and meaning, recover from errors with helpful messages, generate reports, and write automated tests.

sections.heading: Persistent data
paragraphs: Variables disappear when a program closes. Persistent storage keeps data between runs. A JSON file suits small structured data such as settings or a short list of records. A CSV file suits tables that may be opened in a spreadsheet. A database such as SQLite, which is built into Python, suits larger data, searching, and multiple related tables. Plan for missing or damaged files so the program does not crash on first run.

sections.heading: Validate input for format and meaning
paragraphs: Validation has layers. Presence: is the field filled in? Format: is it a number, a date, an email? Range and meaning: is a quantity between 1 and 99, is a pickup date in the future, does an ID exist? Reject bad input with a message that says what is wrong and how to fix it, and let the user try again without losing other entries.
Raise exceptions in small functions and catch them where the program talks to the user. This keeps the validation rule in one place, where it can be tested.
bullets: Empty input, "abc," "-3," and "30" are all rejected with a message; "1.5" is accepted.
Never show users a raw crash trace. Log technical details for yourself and show a plain message to the user.

sections.heading: Generate a report
paragraphs: A report summarizes stored data for a decision: totals by category, counts, averages, and date ranges. Build it from functions that return data, and keep printing or formatting separate, so the same totals can be shown on screen, saved to CSV, or charted.

example.scenario: What does the report print?
example.solution: Math totals 2.00 and Reading totals 1.5 + 0.5 = 2.00. Sorted alphabetically, it prints "Math        2.00" then "Reading     2.00", with names left-aligned in 10 characters and hours right-aligned in 6.

sections.heading: Test automatically
paragraphs: Automated tests check that functions behave correctly and keep working after changes. With the pytest package (install with pip install pytest), any function named test_ in a file named test_*.py runs with the command pytest. Test normal cases, boundary cases (exactly 0.25 and 24), and invalid input. Write a test that reproduces each bug before fixing it.
Also test by hand from the user's view: a checklist of tasks, the expected result, the actual result, and any fix made. This test log is strong evidence in a presentation.

practice.task: Write parse_quantity(text) that returns an int from 1 to 99 or raises ValueError, plus three pytest tests: one valid, one boundary, and one invalid.

Checking that input is present, correctly formatted, and meaningful.
An error signal raised during execution that can be caught and handled.
An automated check of one small piece of code.
An input at the edge of the allowed range.

questions.explanation: Databases store, relate, and search large amounts of data.

questions.prompt: Checking that a pickup date is in the future is validation of:
questions.explanation: A correctly formatted date can still be invalid for the task.

questions.explanation: Boundary tests check the edges of the range.

questions.explanation: Helpful messages let users correct the problem.

questions.prompt: Why write a test before fixing a bug?
choices: It proves the bug exists and later confirms the fix
questions.explanation: The test fails first, then passes after the fix and guards against the bug returning.

modules.title: Interfaces, intelligent features, packaging, and demonstrations
modules.summary: Design usable and accessible interfaces, add an intelligent feature you can explain and evaluate, organize source code, write a README with credits, package a standalone app, and demonstrate against the rubric.

sections.heading: Usable, accessible interfaces
paragraphs: An interface should make the main task obvious. Use clear labels next to every field, sensible defaults, consistent navigation, and short instructions where users might hesitate. Show feedback after every action, such as "Saved" or a specific error beside the field. Group related controls and put the main action where users expect it.

Accessibility means people using keyboards, screen readers, magnification, or color-vision aids can use the program. Every control should work with the keyboard, have a visible focus indicator, and have a text label. Meet contrast requirements, do not rely on color alone, and let text scale. Test with real users: give three to five people a task, watch without helping, and note where they hesitate. Record each problem and the change you made.

sections.heading: Add an intelligent feature you can explain
paragraphs: Some events require an intelligent or advanced feature. Read the current guide's definition before choosing. Options range from simple to complex: rule-based logic, scoring and recommendation, search with ranking, a trained machine learning model, or a call to an AI service. Choose the simplest approach that meets the requirement and that you can explain, test, and run reliably during judging.
The example below recommends items by counting shared tags. It is transparent: you can explain exactly why each recommendation appears.

example.scenario: What does the recommendation code print, and how would you evaluate the feature?
steps: Scores: Atlas 1 (history), Byte 0, Cosmos 2 (space and history), Dune 1 (space).
Sorted by score, then name: Cosmos, Atlas, Dune. Byte is excluded because its score is 0.
example.solution: It prints ['Cosmos', 'Atlas', 'Dune']. To evaluate it, write test cases with expected rankings, ask a few users whether recommendations seem useful, and note limits: it ignores ratings and treats all tags as equally important. If you use an AI service instead, explain what data is sent, how you protect privacy, what happens when the service is unavailable, and how you checked the output's accuracy.

sections.heading: Organize, document, and credit
paragraphs: Organize source code into folders by purpose, with meaningful file and function names and brief comments explaining why, not what. Keep secrets such as API keys out of the code. Use version control such as Git with frequent, descriptive commits; the history also documents your process.

A README explains what the program does, system requirements, how to install and run it, how to use the main features, known limitations, and credits. List every library, template, image, sound, and code sample you used with its license and source. Event rules often restrict templates or require originality, so check them.

sections.heading: Package and demonstrate
paragraphs: A standalone build runs without installing a programming language. For Python, PyInstaller can bundle a program: pyinstaller --onefile --windowed app.py creates an executable in the dist folder. Test the build on a different computer before the event, since missing files and paths are common failures. Keep a backup copy on a second device or storage.

Plan the demonstration around the rubric. Show the main user path first, then the required features, the intelligent feature with an explanation, validation and error handling, accessibility, and the code structure. Have test data loaded so you do not type during judging. Practice answering "How does this part work?" by pointing to the specific function.

practice.task: Write a README outline for a small program you could build, such as a study-session tracker. Include at least six section headings and one sentence under each.
practice.answer: Sample: Overview: what the program does and for whom. Requirements: operating system and anything to install. Installation: how to run the packaged app or source. Using the app: the main tasks step by step. Data and privacy: where data is saved and what is collected. Testing: how to run the tests and what they cover. Known limitations: what it does not do yet. Credits and licenses: every library and asset with its license. A strong outline lets a judge run and understand the program without the author present.

terms.definition: Watching real users attempt tasks to find where an interface confuses them.
A document explaining how to install, run, and use a program.
A packaged program that runs without installing its programming language.
A system such as Git that records changes to code over time.
A program that makes decisions using explicit if-then rules.

questions.prompt: Which interface choice supports keyboard and screen reader users?
choices: Labels on every control and visible focus
questions.explanation: Labels and focus indicators make controls usable without a mouse or sight.

questions.prompt: Why test a packaged build on a different computer?
choices: To catch missing files and settings that worked only on yours
questions.explanation: Your own machine may hide dependencies the build lacks.

choices: Out of the source code, such as in a private settings file
questions.explanation: Keys in shared code can be stolen and misused.

questions.prompt: Why choose a simple, explainable intelligent feature?
choices: You can explain, test, and run it reliably during judging
questions.explanation: Understanding and reliability matter as much as sophistication.

choices: Every library and asset used with its license

modules.title: Game and simulation development: loop, state, rules, and playtesting
modules.summary: Build a game loop with input, update, and draw; manage states and multiple outcomes; design mechanics and instructions; playtest for accessibility; and build, credit, and document a standalone game.

sections.heading: The game loop
paragraphs: Every real-time game repeats one loop many times a second: handle input, update the game state, draw the screen, and wait so the loop runs at a steady frame rate such as 60 frames per second. The state is all the data that describes the game at a moment: positions, score, health, time left, and which screen is showing.

The example uses pygame, a free Python library (pip install pygame). The player moves with the arrow keys and collects a coin; each coin raises the score and moves the coin. Collision uses axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABB): two rectangles overlap if each one's left edge is left of the other's right edge and each one's top edge is above the other's bottom edge. pygame's colliderect does this check.

code.content:
import pygame

pygame.init()
screen = pygame.display.set_mode((640, 480))
clock = pygame.time.Clock()
player = pygame.Rect(300, 400, 40, 40)
coin = pygame.Rect(100, 100, 20, 20)
score, running = 0, True

while running:
    for event in pygame.event.get():          # 1. input
        if event.type == pygame.QUIT:
            running = False
    keys = pygame.key.get_pressed()
    player.x += (keys[pygame.K_RIGHT] - keys[pygame.K_LEFT]) * 5
    player.y += (keys[pygame.K_DOWN] - keys[pygame.K_UP]) * 5
    player.clamp_ip(screen.get_rect())        # 2. update
    if player.colliderect(coin):
        score += 1
        coin.topleft = (score * 97 % 600, score * 53 % 440)
    screen.fill((20, 30, 40))                 # 3. draw
    pygame.draw.rect(screen, (80, 200, 120), player)
    pygame.draw.rect(screen, (240, 200, 60), coin)
    pygame.display.flip()
    clock.tick(60)                            # 4. wait

pygame.quit()

sections.heading: States, rules, and multiple outcomes
paragraphs: A state machine organizes screens and modes: MENU, INSTRUCTIONS, PLAYING, PAUSED, WIN, and LOSE. Each state handles its own input, update, and drawing, and clear rules move between states, such as "if score reaches 10, go to WIN; if the timer reaches 0, go to LOSE." This prevents bugs such as the player moving while paused.

Simulations model a system with rules, such as a store's customers arriving each minute with some probability. Use a fixed random seed while testing so results are repeatable, then remove it for play. Multiple outcomes, such as winning, losing, or different endings based on choices, give players reasons to replay. Every outcome needs a clear screen explaining what happened and how to play again.

example.scenario: Design the states for a 60-second coin game with a win and a lose condition.
steps: MENU: show title, Start, Instructions, and Quit; Enter starts the game.
INSTRUCTIONS: explain controls and goal; Escape returns to MENU.
PLAYING: timer counts down from 60; collecting 15 coins goes to WIN; reaching 0 seconds goes to LOSE; P goes to PAUSED.
PAUSED: freeze the timer and movement; P resumes.
WIN and LOSE: show the score and time, with Play Again and Menu options.
example.solution: Writing the states and transitions before coding makes the rules testable: each arrow in the diagram becomes a test case, such as "pressing P during PLAYING stops the timer."

sections.heading: Design, accessibility, and playtesting
paragraphs: Connect the assigned topic to the mechanics, meaning what the player does, not just to the artwork. Define the goal, the challenge that makes it hard, how difficulty rises, and the completion condition. Teach controls through instructions and an easy first level.

Accessible games offer remappable controls, adjustable difficulty, pause at any time, subtitles or visual cues for important sounds, color choices that work for color-blind players, and no required rapid button pressing without an alternative. Playtest with people who have not seen the game: watch silently, note where they get stuck, ask what they thought the goal was, and record each change you made in a playtest log with the date, the problem, and the fix.

sections.heading: Assets, performance, builds, and process evidence
paragraphs: Create your own art and sound or use assets whose licenses allow your use, and credit them. Check performance with a frame rate display; drawing thousands of objects or loading images inside the loop slows games. Load assets once, before the loop. Recover from errors: if a save file is missing or damaged, start a new game instead of crashing.

Build a standalone version with the engine's export tool (such as PyInstaller for pygame, or the export features in Godot or Unity) and test it on another computer. Keep process evidence: design documents, state diagrams, version history, playtest logs, and bug lists. Use them for any progress report required at an earlier stage and in the final demonstration, organized by the rating sheet.

practice.task: Write the AABB overlap test for rectangles a and b, each with x, y (top-left corner), w, and h. Then check: a = (10, 10, 20, 20) and b = (25, 15, 10, 10). Do they overlap?
practice.answer: Overlap if a.x < b.x + b.w and b.x < a.x + a.w and a.y < b.y + b.h and b.y < a.y + a.h. Check: 10 < 35, 25 < 30, 10 < 25, and 15 < 30 are all true, so they overlap. b's left edge (25) is inside a, which spans x from 10 to 30.

terms.definition: The repeating cycle of input, update, and draw that runs a game.
All the data describing a game at a given moment.
A design that defines a set of modes and the rules for switching between them.
Detecting overlap between axis-aligned rectangles.
A dated record of problems observed in testing and the changes made.

questions.prompt: What is the usual order inside a game loop?
questions.explanation: Read input, change the state, then show the new state.

questions.prompt: Why load images before the loop rather than inside it?
questions.explanation: Loading inside the loop repeats expensive work dozens of times a second.

questions.prompt: A PAUSED state should:
questions.explanation: Pausing stops updates until the player resumes.

questions.prompt: Which feature improves accessibility?
questions.explanation: Options let more players adapt the game to their needs.

questions.prompt: Why use a fixed random seed during testing?
questions.explanation: The same seed produces the same random sequence each run.

modules.title: Mobile app development: platforms, screens, data, and device testing
modules.summary: Choose a supported platform, build screens with navigation and state, store data on the device, handle permissions and small-screen accessibility, test on a real phone, and document the app.

sections.heading: Choose a platform
paragraphs: The captured Mobile Application Development guide still names Windows Phone, which Microsoft no longer supports. Check the current national guidance for accepted platforms before choosing, and confirm the decision with your adviser.

Native development builds separately for each platform with its own tools. Cross-platform frameworks share one codebase across iOS and Android. Beginners can prototype with block-based tools such as MIT App Inventor.

rows: Requires a Mac with Xcode; free personal provisioning allows testing on your own iPhone
Android Studio runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux
One codebase; iOS builds still need a Mac
Fast prototyping; limited for complex apps

sections.heading: Screens, navigation, state, and storage
paragraphs: Sketch every screen and the path between them before coding: a home screen, list screens, detail screens, forms, and settings. Mobile navigation is usually a stack (push a detail screen, then go back) plus tabs for top-level sections. Keep the back behavior predictable.

State is the data the screen shows, such as the list of items and whether a form is valid. When state changes, the framework redraws the affected parts of the screen. Store data that must survive closing the app on the device: key-value storage for small settings, and a local database such as SQLite (Room on Android, Core Data or SwiftData on iOS) for lists of records. If the app syncs to the internet, decide what happens offline.

example.scenario: Plan the screens for a fictional plant-watering reminder app.
steps: Tab 1, My Plants: a list showing each plant's name, photo, and days until watering. Tapping a plant opens Plant Detail.
Plant Detail: watering schedule, last watered date, and a large "Watered today" button.
Add Plant form: name (required), watering interval in days (1 to 30), optional photo.
Tab 2, Settings: reminder time and notification permission status.
Storage: a local database table of plants; reminders scheduled with the operating system's notification service.
example.solution: Each screen has one main job, the form validates the interval, and the data stays on the device, so the app works offline. Notification permission is requested only when the user turns reminders on, with an explanation.

sections.heading: Small screens, touch, permissions, and errors
paragraphs: Design for one hand and small screens. Touch targets should be at least 44 by 44 points on iOS and 48 by 48 density-independent pixels on Android. Support the system text size setting, keep contrast high, label icons for screen readers (VoiceOver on iOS, TalkBack on Android), and avoid information conveyed only by color or gesture.

Request permissions such as location, camera, or notifications at the moment they are needed, with a short explanation of why, and keep the app usable if the user says no. Handle errors visibly: show a clear message when the network is unavailable, keep entered data when a save fails, and offer a retry.

sections.heading: Test on devices and document
paragraphs: Emulators are useful, but test on a real phone before judging. Check different screen sizes, landscape orientation if supported, slow or no network, low battery mode, the app being closed and reopened, and large text. Watch for crashes and record them with steps to reproduce. Measure launch time and scrolling smoothness on an older device if possible.

Build a requirement-by-requirement checklist from the current guide and mark where the app meets each one. Write a README, list every library and asset with its license, and prepare a demonstration that installs or runs the app on a device, shows each required feature, and explains design and code choices.

practice.task: Write five test cases for the plant app's Add Plant form, each with input and expected result.
practice.answer: 1. Name "Fern," interval 7: saves and appears in the list showing 7 days. 2. Name blank: shows "Enter a plant name" and does not save. 3. Interval 0: shows "Choose 1 to 30 days." 4. Interval 31: same message. 5. Valid plant entered with airplane mode on: saves locally and appears after the app is closed and reopened. Strong answers include boundary values (1 and 30) and an offline case.

A tool that builds apps for several platforms from one codebase.
A pattern where screens are pushed on top of each other and removed when the user goes back.
The tappable area of a control.
Software that imitates a phone on a computer for testing.

choices: When the feature that needs it is used, with an explanation
questions.explanation: Asking in context explains the need and increases trust.

choices: A local database such as SQLite
questions.explanation: A database keeps structured data after the app closes.

questions.prompt: Building an iOS app with SwiftUI requires:
questions.explanation: Apple's tools run on macOS.

choices: Real devices reveal performance, touch, and hardware issues

modules.title: Hands-on web development: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and testing
modules.summary: Write semantic, accessible HTML, build responsive layouts with CSS, add validated interactive features with JavaScript and saved state, debug in the browser, test across devices, and deploy original code.

sections.heading: Structure with semantic HTML
paragraphs: HTML describes what content is. Semantic elements such as header, nav, main, section, article, and footer give structure that browsers, search engines, and screen readers understand. Use one h1 per page and headings in order. Every image needs an alt attribute describing its purpose (empty alt="" for decoration). Every form field needs a label element linked by for and id.

Shared navigation should be identical on every page, with the current page marked using aria-current="page". Include the viewport meta tag, meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1", so pages scale on phones.

code.content:
Home Events

Upcoming events

...
Contact: club@example.org

sections.heading: Responsive layout with CSS
paragraphs: Write styles mobile-first: a single-column layout by default, then media queries add columns on wider screens. Flexbox arranges items in one direction, such as a navigation bar. Grid arranges two-dimensional layouts, such as cards. Use relative units (rem, %) so text and spacing scale. Keep a visible focus style for keyboard users, and check color contrast.

sections.heading: Interaction, validation, and saved state
paragraphs: JavaScript responds to events such as clicks and form submissions. Validate on the page for a fast, helpful experience, and validate again on the server if there is one, since browser checks can be bypassed. Show errors next to the field in text, and announce them to screen readers with aria-live. Insert user text with textContent, never innerHTML, to prevent script injection.

localStorage saves small amounts of data in the browser so it survives a page reload. It is stored only on that browser and device, so it is not a substitute for a database when users need shared or secure data.

example.scenario: A user submits the form empty, then types "sam@" and submits, then types "sam@example.org" and submits, then reloads the page. What happens?
steps: Empty: validity fails because the field is required; the error message appears and focus returns to the field.
"sam@": validity fails because it is not a complete email; the same message appears.
"sam@example.org": the error clears, the address is saved to localStorage, added to the list, and the form resets.
Reload: the saved array is read from localStorage and the address appears in the list again.
example.solution: The page validates presence and format, explains the fix in text, keeps keyboard focus sensible, and persists the result in the browser.

sections.heading: Debug, test, deploy, and document
paragraphs: Browser developer tools (F12 or right-click, Inspect) show the HTML and CSS applied to each element, JavaScript errors in the Console, network requests and failed files in the Network tab, and device emulation for different screen sizes. Read the first error in the Console and its line number.

Test on desktop, tablet, and phone sizes and in at least two browsers. Check every link, test keyboard-only navigation (Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter), run an automated accessibility and performance audit such as Lighthouse, and compress large images. Record each test, its result, and any fix in a test log.

Deploy to a static host such as GitHub Pages or Netlify, or follow the event's submission rules. Website Coding and Development prohibits website templates, so write your own HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and credit any libraries, fonts, and images with their licenses. Comment code where the reason is not obvious, and keep version history as evidence of original work.

practice.task: Add a second field to the form: a required "Name" field with a label and its own error message. Write the HTML for the field and the JavaScript check that runs before the email check.
practice.answer:
HTML:

Using trim rejects names that are only spaces, which the required attribute alone allows.

A CSS rule that applies styles at certain screen sizes or conditions.
Writing base styles for small screens and adding layouts for larger ones.

questions.explanation: textContent treats input as text, not HTML or code.

questions.explanation: Grid handles two-dimensional layouts.

questions.explanation: The Console lists errors with file and line numbers.

questions.explanation: Client-side checks help users, but only server checks protect data.

modules.title: Website design process: research, wireframes, build, testing, and success measures
modules.summary: Research the audience, plan content and navigation, wireframe and design consistent pages, build in a permitted tool, test on three device categories, and measure and present success.

sections.heading: Research and plan content
paragraphs: Start with the people the site serves and the tasks they come to do. Research through short interviews or surveys and by studying similar sites. Write two or three user tasks, such as "Find this week's volunteer opportunities and sign up in under two minutes." These tasks guide every design decision and become your test plan. This lesson uses a fictional community garden site, unrelated to the competition topic.

Make a content inventory listing every piece of content needed, who provides it, and where it lives. Group content by what users look for, not by how the organization is structured. Draw a sitemap showing pages and their hierarchy, and keep important pages no more than two or three clicks from home.

sections.heading: Wireframes and visual design
paragraphs: Wireframes are simple layouts showing where content and controls go, without colors or images. Start with low-fidelity sketches for each page type, including the phone layout, then make higher-fidelity mockups. Get feedback on wireframes, when changes are cheap.

Visual design applies hierarchy, a consistent grid, a limited color palette with accessible contrast, and one or two typefaces. Keep navigation, headers, and footers identical on every page. Write in plain language with short paragraphs and descriptive headings and link text ("View the planting calendar" instead of "Click here"). Cite sources for facts and credit images.

example.scenario: Explain two design decisions for the community garden home page.
example.solution: Decision 1: the "Volunteer this week" button sits at the top of the home page in the accent color, because interviews showed volunteering was the most common reason people visit. Decision 2: the phone layout stacks the calendar below the button and hides secondary links in a labeled menu, because four of five testers used phones. Each decision cites research and a user task.

sections.heading: Build and add interactive elements
paragraphs: Build in a tool the current event guide permits, and confirm whether site builders, templates, or hand-coded pages are allowed. Create the required pages and working interactive elements such as forms, filters, maps, or calendars. Every interactive element needs clear labels, keyboard access, visible feedback, and helpful error messages. Include a friendly page for broken links (a 404 page) that offers a way back.

sections.heading: Test, measure, and present
paragraphs: Test on at least three device categories, such as desktop, tablet, and phone, and in more than one browser. Check readability, layout, links, forms, and loading speed. Run usability tests: give five people your user tasks, watch without helping, and record whether they succeed, how long it takes, and where they hesitate. Keep a testing record with dates, results, and the revision made for each problem.

Define success measures before launch, such as task completion rate, time on task, form submissions, or the share of visitors who reach the volunteer page. Present the site by walking through the research, planning artifacts (sitemap and wireframes), key design decisions and their reasons, implementation, testing results and revisions, and how success would be measured.

sections.heading: A troubleshooting method you can defend
paragraphs: Diagnosis should follow evidence, not a memorized symptom list. The widely taught six-step method works for any fault. Back up data before changes that could lose it, and change one thing at a time so you know what fixed the problem.
steps: Identify the problem: ask the user what changed, when it started, and what they see; reproduce it; check logs.
Establish a theory of probable cause, starting with the simple and obvious.
Test the theory. If it is wrong, form a new theory or escalate.
Establish a plan of action and implement the fix, considering business impact and policies.
Verify full system functionality and add preventive measures.
Document the symptoms, cause, fix, and outcome.

sections.heading: Boot process, file systems, and system internals
paragraphs: At power-on, firmware (UEFI on modern systems, BIOS on older ones) runs the power-on self-test (POST), finds a boot device using the boot order, and starts a boot loader such as Windows Boot Manager or GRUB on Linux. The boot loader loads the operating system kernel, which starts drivers and services and shows the login screen. Failures at each stage look different: beeps or no display point to POST and hardware; "no boot device" points to boot order or the drive; a crash after the logo points to drivers or system files.

The registry is Windows' hierarchical database of system and application settings, with main branches such as HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE (computer-wide) and HKEY_CURRENT_USER. Back it up before editing with regedit; a wrong change can stop Windows from starting. Virtual memory uses a page file on the drive to extend RAM. Constant paging, visible as high disk activity with slow response, usually means the system needs more RAM.

sections.heading: Utilities, installs, and crashes
paragraphs: Windows utilities include Task Manager (processes, performance, startup apps), Event Viewer (system and application logs), Device Manager (drivers and hardware status), Disk Management, Services, System Configuration (msconfig), and Resource Monitor. macOS has Activity Monitor, Disk Utility, and Console. Safe Mode starts Windows with minimal drivers, which helps isolate driver and startup problems.

Before installing or upgrading an operating system, check hardware requirements, back up data, confirm license and driver availability, and decide between an in-place upgrade (keeps files and apps) and a clean install (erases the drive, removes accumulated problems). A Windows stop error (blue screen) shows a stop code; note it, check Event Viewer and recent driver or update changes, and test memory and storage. A macOS or Linux kernel panic is the equivalent.

example.scenario: A laptop cannot load websites. ipconfig shows IPv4 address 169.254.37.12 and no default gateway.
steps: 169.254.x.x is an automatic private (APIPA) address. Windows assigns it when it cannot reach a DHCP server.
Theory: the laptop is not getting an address from DHCP. Check the Wi-Fi connection or cable, then the router or DHCP server.

Verify: ipconfig now shows 192.168.1.47 with gateway 192.168.1.1, and websites load.
example.solution: Document that the laptop had joined a guest network without DHCP, and the fix was reconnecting to the staff network. The address range was the key evidence.

practice.task: Interpret each result and name the most likely problem: (a) ping 8.8.8.8 succeeds, but ping example.com says it could not find the host. (b) ping 192.168.1.1 (the gateway) fails, but other laptops work, and the network cable's light is off. (c) tracert to a website stops responding after the third hop, but the site loads in a browser.

(b) A physical layer problem on this laptop's connection: check the cable, port, and network adapter. (c) Probably not a problem: many routers do not answer traceroute probes even while forwarding traffic, which is why the site still loads.

sections.heading: Components and performance
paragraphs: The CPU executes instructions; more cores help multitasking and heavy applications, and clock speed affects single-task speed. RAM holds running programs; too little causes slowdowns as the system pages to disk. Storage keeps data: hard disk drives (HDDs) spin platters and are slow but cheap per gigabyte; SATA solid-state drives (SSDs) reach roughly 550 MB/s; NVMe SSDs in M.2 slots reach several gigabytes per second. The power supply (PSU) converts wall power and must provide enough wattage with headroom. The motherboard's form factor (ATX, microATX, Mini-ITX) and socket determine compatible parts.

Upgrade decisions start with evidence. If Task Manager shows memory near 100% during normal work, add RAM of the type and speed the motherboard supports. If the system has an HDD, moving to an SSD is usually the largest improvement users notice. Check compatibility: CPU socket and chipset, RAM generation (DDR4 and DDR5 are not interchangeable), free slots, physical size, and power.

sections.heading: Power and startup faults
paragraphs: For a computer that shows no sign of power, check the obvious first: the outlet, the power strip switch, the PSU's rear switch, and the cable. If the fans spin but there is no display, check the monitor input and cable, reseat RAM, and listen for beep codes or read the motherboard's diagnostic lights. Random shutdowns under load often point to overheating (clogged vents, failed fan, dried thermal paste) or a failing PSU. Swollen capacitors on a board indicate hardware failure. Use proper electrostatic discharge (ESD) precautions, such as a grounded wrist strap, when working inside a computer.

sections.heading: Laptops and mobile devices
paragraphs: Laptop batteries wear with charge cycles; system reports show design capacity versus current capacity. A swollen battery is a fire risk: power down, stop using it, and replace it. Heat problems come from blocked vents and dust; keep laptops on hard surfaces. Many laptops allow replacing RAM and SSDs, but some solder these to the board, so check before promising an upgrade.

Mobile devices synchronize email, contacts, and calendars through accounts such as Microsoft 365, Google, or iCloud. Sync problems often come from expired passwords, disabled sync settings, or no data connection. Bluetooth problems: confirm both devices have Bluetooth on and the accessory is in pairing mode, stay within range (often about 10 meters), "forget" and re-pair the device, and check battery levels. Cellular problems: check signal strength and airplane mode, restart, check the SIM or eSIM and carrier account, and verify the access point name (APN) settings if data fails while calls work.

sections.heading: Printers
paragraphs: A laser printer uses seven steps: processing (the image is prepared in memory), charging (the drum receives a uniform charge), exposing (a laser writes the image onto the drum), developing (toner sticks to the exposed areas), transferring (toner moves to the paper), fusing (heat and pressure melt the toner onto the paper), and cleaning (leftover toner is removed from the drum). Inkjet printers spray liquid ink through nozzles. Thermal printers use heat-sensitive paper for receipts and labels. Impact printers strike a ribbon and can print multipart forms.

Network printers should have a fixed address through a static IP or a DHCP reservation so computers can always find them. A stuck print queue is often cleared by restarting the Print Spooler service on Windows. Garbled output usually means a wrong or corrupt driver.

example.solution: Evidence points to the fusing step: toner reaches the paper but is not melted on. Check the maintenance counter and replace the fuser assembly after it cools, then print test pages and confirm the toner no longer rubs off. Document the page count so the next replacement can be planned.

(b) The earbuds may be paired only to the phone. Turn off Bluetooth on the phone or disconnect there, put the earbuds in pairing mode, then forget and re-pair them on the laptop. (c) Check that mobile data is turned on and airplane mode is off, then verify the APN settings and the carrier account.
