sections.heading: Property, terms, and valuation
paragraphs: Real property is land and anything permanently attached to it; personal property is movable. A fixture is personal property attached so that it becomes part of the real property, such as a built-in dishwasher. Other key terms include an easement (a right to use someone else's land, such as a utility line), an encroachment (something that extends onto a neighbor's land), a lien (a claim against property for a debt), and equity (value minus what is owed). Property types include residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural, special-purpose, and vacant land. Zoning controls land use.

Appraisers use three approaches. The sales comparison approach adjusts recent sales of similar properties (comparables) for differences. The cost approach adds land value to the cost of replacing the building, minus depreciation; it suits new or unusual buildings. The income approach divides net operating income (NOI) by a capitalization rate; it suits rental properties.

example.scenario: A 12-unit apartment building rents for $1,500 per unit per month. Vacancy is 5%, operating expenses are $82,000 a year, and similar buildings sell at a 7% cap rate. Estimate its value.
steps: Potential gross income: 12 x 1,500 x 12 = $216,000.
Effective gross income: 216,000 x 95% = $205,200.
example.solution: Estimated value is $1,760,000. Note that NOI excludes mortgage payments, and a higher cap rate would produce a lower value.

sections.heading: Careers, licensing, and regulators
paragraphs: A real estate agent (salesperson) must work under a licensed broker. A broker has more education and experience, can operate independently, and supervises agents. A REALTOR is a member of the National Association of REALTORS who agrees to its Code of Ethics. Licensing generally requires prelicensing education, a state exam, a background check, and, for agents, a sponsoring broker, plus continuing education; in Maryland, the State Real Estate Commission licenses and disciplines licensees. Other careers include property manager, appraiser, home inspector, mortgage loan officer, title examiner, and developer, and many agents run their own businesses.

Federal agencies matter too: HUD enforces the Fair Housing Act, and the CFPB enforces mortgage disclosure rules, including the Loan Estimate given after application and the Closing Disclosure given at least three business days before closing. Rules change; for example, a 2024 legal settlement changed how buyer agent compensation is offered and led to required written agreements with buyers before touring homes. Check current rules and dates before relying on them.

sections.heading: Fair housing, disclosures, and tenancy
paragraphs: The federal Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination in housing based on race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, and disability. Maryland and many localities add protected classes; check current state and county law. Prohibited practices include steering (guiding buyers toward or away from neighborhoods based on protected traits), blockbusting, redlining, and discriminatory advertising. Advertisements should describe the property, not the kind of person wanted.

Sellers and landlords of housing built before 1978 must disclose known lead-based paint hazards and provide the EPA pamphlet. States require additional property condition disclosures. Leases may be fixed-term or month-to-month; landlord and tenant duties and security deposit rules come from state and local law.

Ways to hold title include ownership in severalty (one owner), tenancy in common (shares that pass by will), joint tenancy with right of survivorship (surviving owners inherit automatically), and tenancy by the entirety (a form for married couples in states that recognize it, including Maryland).

sections.heading: From listing to closing
steps: Listing: the seller signs a listing agreement; the agent prepares a comparative market analysis to suggest a price and markets the property.
Offer and acceptance: the buyer's purchase agreement states price, earnest money deposit, contingencies (financing, inspection, appraisal), and closing date.
Due diligence: home inspection, appraisal for the lender, and a title search; title insurance protects against past defects.
Financing: the lender underwrites and approves the loan.
Final walkthrough and closing (called settlement in Maryland): documents are signed, funds are disbursed, and the deed is recorded in public land records.
paragraphs: Deeds transfer ownership. A general warranty deed gives the most protection, promising clear title against all past claims. A special warranty deed covers only the seller's period of ownership. A quitclaim deed transfers whatever interest the grantor has, with no promises.

Most buyers borrow. A conventional loan with less than 20% down usually requires private mortgage insurance; FHA, VA, and USDA loans are government-backed options. Rates may be fixed or adjustable, and points are fees paid to lower the rate. In the secondary mortgage market, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac buy conforming loans from lenders, and Ginnie Mae guarantees securities backed by government loans, which gives lenders cash to make new loans. Investors compare rental property (cash flow and appreciation, with management work), REITs (liquid and diversified), and renovation projects (higher risk).

sections.heading: Agency and ethics
paragraphs: An agent who represents a client owes fiduciary duties, often remembered as OLDCAR: obedience to lawful instructions, loyalty, disclosure of material facts, confidentiality, accounting for funds, and reasonable care. A seller's agent represents the seller; a buyer's agent represents the buyer. Dual agency, representing both sides, creates a conflict and requires informed written consent where it is allowed. Commercial representation often involves leases, investment analysis, and zoning issues that residential agents rarely handle.

Listing advertising must be truthful, comply with fair housing, and include required brokerage information. Ethical cases often involve disclosure, such as an agent who knows of a leaking roof, or confidentiality, such as a seller's agent revealing the seller's lowest acceptable price.

practice.task: (a) A seller's agent tells a buyer, "My sellers are desperate and will take $20,000 less." Which duty is breached? (b) An agent suggests to a family with young children that they look only in a neighborhood "with lots of other families like yours." What is the problem? (c) A home built in 1965 is for sale. What federal disclosure applies?
practice.answer: (a) Confidentiality and loyalty owed to the seller. (b) Steering based on familial status, which violates the Fair Housing Act; the agent should show homes matching the buyers' stated criteria everywhere. (c) The lead-based paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing, including known hazards, available records, the EPA pamphlet, and the buyer's opportunity for an inspection.

modules.title: Project management documents: charter to closure, with schedule and earned value math
modules.summary: Write a charter and stakeholder plan, define scope and acceptance criteria, build a WBS and critical path, plan resources, quality, communication, and risk, track with earned value, manage change, and close formally.

sections.heading: Initiate: charter, stakeholders, and scope
paragraphs: A project is a temporary effort to create a unique result. It moves through initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, and closing. The project charter authorizes the project: it states the purpose, measurable objectives, high-level scope, key milestones, budget, sponsor, and the project manager's authority.

Stakeholders are anyone affected by or able to affect the project. A stakeholder register lists each one with their interests, influence, and expectations; a power-interest grid helps decide whom to manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, or monitor. The project manager is responsible for planning, coordinating, communicating, and delivering within constraints, and follows professional ethics such as PMI's values of responsibility, respect, fairness, and honesty.

The scope statement describes deliverables, what is excluded, assumptions, and constraints. Acceptance criteria state how each deliverable will be judged complete, such as "The registration site handles 300 sign-ups with no errors in testing."

sections.heading: Plan: WBS, schedule, and critical path
paragraphs: A work breakdown structure (WBS) breaks the total scope into deliverables and then into work packages small enough to estimate and assign. Under the 100% rule, the WBS includes all the work and only the work. Estimate durations by analogy with past projects, by parametric rates (such as hours per page), or with three-point estimates: (optimistic + 4 x most likely + pessimistic) / 6.

Dependencies connect tasks; finish-to-start (B cannot start until A finishes) is the most common. The critical path is the longest path through the network, and it sets the shortest possible project duration. Tasks on it have zero float; a delay to any of them delays the project.

example.scenario: Tasks: A (3 days, first), B (5 days, after A), C (2 days, after A), D (4 days, after C), E (2 days, after both B and D). Find the critical path.
steps: Path A-B-E: 3 + 5 + 2 = 10 days.
Path A-C-D-E: 3 + 2 + 4 + 2 = 11 days.
The longest path is A-C-D-E at 11 days, so it is critical. Task B has 11 - 10 = 1 day of float.
example.solution: The project takes 11 days. To finish sooner, shorten C or D (for example, by adding resources, called crashing, or overlapping tasks, called fast tracking); shortening B would not help.

bullets: Resource plan: who and what each task needs, and when; watch for one person assigned to overlapping tasks.
Quality plan: standards, checks, and who approves each deliverable.
Communication plan: who needs what information, how often, and in what format.
Risk register: each risk's probability, impact, owner, and response (avoid, mitigate, transfer, or accept; for opportunities, exploit or enhance).

sections.heading: Build and update the plan in project software
steps: Enter tasks from the WBS with durations.
Link dependencies; the software calculates dates and highlights the critical path.
Assign resources and check for overallocation.
Save a baseline, a snapshot of the approved plan.
Each week, enter actual progress and costs and compare with the baseline in a Gantt chart or variance report.
Use the comparison to decide on corrective actions and report status.
paragraphs: Microsoft Project, Smartsheet, and many free tools follow the same pattern, and a spreadsheet can do the same for small projects. The baseline is what makes tracking meaningful.

sections.heading: Execute and control: teams, changes, and earned value
paragraphs: Teams typically move through forming, storming, norming, performing, and adjourning. Cross-functional teams need clear roles, shared goals, and regular communication; motivation comes from meaningful work, recognition, and removing obstacles. Changes to scope, schedule, or budget go through a change control process: submit a change request, analyze its impact, get approval from the designated authority, update the plan, and communicate it. Uncontrolled additions are called scope creep.

Earned value management compares planned work, completed work, and cost. Planned value (PV) is the budgeted cost of work scheduled to date. Earned value (EV) is the budgeted cost of work actually completed. Actual cost (AC) is what was spent. Cost variance = EV - AC; schedule variance = EV - PV. The cost performance index (CPI) = EV / AC and the schedule performance index (SPI) = EV / PV; below 1 is unfavorable.

practice.task: A $100,000 project should be 50% complete by now. It is actually 40% complete, and $45,000 has been spent. Calculate PV, EV, AC, CV, SV, CPI, and SPI, and state what they mean.
practice.answer: PV = $50,000; EV = 40% x 100,000 = $40,000; AC = $45,000. CV = 40,000 - 45,000 = -$5,000 (over budget). SV = 40,000 - 50,000 = -$10,000 (behind schedule). CPI = 40,000 / 45,000 = 0.89; SPI = 40,000 / 50,000 = 0.80. The project gets 89 cents of planned work per dollar spent and is progressing at 80% of the planned rate, so the manager should investigate causes and consider corrective action.

sections.heading: Close the project
paragraphs: Closing confirms that deliverables are accepted, preferably with written sign-off against the acceptance criteria. Evaluate results against the charter's objectives, budget, and schedule. Recognize team members' contributions. Hold a lessons-learned session asking what went well, what did not, and what to change, and record the answers where future teams will find them. Archive project records, hand deliverables over to the people who will operate or maintain them, close contracts, and release resources. A project that skips closing often leaves loose ends and repeats the same mistakes.
